Assume the marginal identity $p_t(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}p_s(x)q(s,x;t,y)\,dx$ and the Chapman–Kolmogorov identity $q(s,x;t,y)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}q(s,x;r,z)q(r,z;t,y)\,dz$ whenever $s<r<t$. For $0\le u<v\le T$ define
$$K_{u,v}(y,A)=\frac{\int_A p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)\,dx}{p_{T-u}(y)}\qquad(A\subseteq\mathbb R^d\text{ Borel}),$$
and set $K_{u,u}(y,\cdot)=\delta_y$. This is the Bayes-reversed transition probability kernel from reverse time $u$ to reverse time $v$; its source state $y$ is the forward-time state at $T-u$ and its output $x$ is the state at $T-v$.

Assume AC. Let $X$ be a continuous Markov process on $[0,T]$ in $\mathbb R^d$, with positive $C^{1,2}$ marginal densities $p_r$ and positive transition densities $q(s,x;r,y)$ satisfying the marginal and Chapman–Kolmogorov identities. For each fixed $(s,x)$, suppose the forward density equation for $q(s,x;\cdot,\cdot)$ holds classically in the evolving time and state variables on $(s,T]\times\mathbb R^d$, and suppose the forward equation for $p$ holds classically, for $L_rf=b_r\cdot\nabla f+\tfrac12a_r:D^2f$ and its formal adjoint $L_r^*$. Put
$$D_rf=p_r^{-1}\{L_r^*(p_rf)-fL_r^*p_r\}=c_r\cdot\nabla f+\tfrac12a_r:D^2f,\qquad c_r=-b_r+p_r^{-1}\nabla\!\cdot(p_ra_r).$$
Assume the displayed coefficients are Borel. On an auxiliary usual filtered probability space, let $Z$ be a continuous Brownian Itô process with initial law $p_T(y)dy$, drift $c_{T-u}(Z_u)$ and bracket density $a_{T-u}(Z_u)$; its drift and diffusion energy integrals are pathwise finite on $[0,T]$. Suppose there are stopping times $\tau_n\uparrow T$ almost surely such that the finite measures
$$\mu_n(E)=E\int_0^{\tau_n}1_E(u,Z_u)du$$
are absolutely continuous with respect to spacetime Lebesgue measure. No marginal law of $Z$ after time zero is assumed.

Then $Z$ has the same path law as $Y_u=X_{T-u}$. In particular its marginal at $u$ is $p_{T-u}$ and its transition kernel from $u$ to $v>u$ is
$$K_{u,v}(y,dx)=\frac{p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)}{p_{T-u}(y)}dx.$$
Consequently $Y$ solves the local martingale problem for $D_{T-u}$ in its natural reversed filtration. The occupation condition is an explicit hypothesis of this intermediate lemma; its applicability must be proved, not inferred from density notation.

Assume AC. Let $X$ be a continuous Markov process on $[0,T]$ in $\mathbb R^d$, with positive $C^{1,2}$ marginal densities $p_r$ and positive transition densities $q(s,x;r,y)$ satisfying the marginal and Chapman–Kolmogorov identities. For each fixed $(s,x)$, suppose the forward density equation for $q(s,x;\cdot,\cdot)$ holds classically in the evolving time and state variables on $(s,T]\times\mathbb R^d$, and suppose the forward equation for $p$ holds classically, for $L_rf=b_r\cdot\nabla f+\tfrac12a_r:D^2f$ and its formal adjoint $L_r^*$. Put
$$D_rf=p_r^{-1}\{L_r^*(p_rf)-fL_r^*p_r\}=c_r\cdot\nabla f+\tfrac12a_r:D^2f,\qquad c_r=-b_r+p_r^{-1}\nabla\!\cdot(p_ra_r).$$
Assume the displayed coefficients are Borel. On an auxiliary usual filtered probability space, let $Z$ be a continuous Brownian Itô process with initial law $p_T(y)dy$, drift $c_{T-u}(Z_u)$ and bracket density $a_{T-u}(Z_u)$; its drift and diffusion energy integrals are pathwise finite on $[0,T]$. Suppose there are stopping times $\tau_n\uparrow T$ almost surely such that the finite measures
$$\mu_n(E)=E\int_0^{\tau_n}1_E(u,Z_u)du$$
are absolutely continuous with respect to spacetime Lebesgue measure. No marginal law of $Z$ after time zero is assumed.

Then $Z$ has the same path law as $Y_u=X_{T-u}$. In particular its marginal at $u$ is $p_{T-u}$ and its transition kernel from $u$ to $v>u$ is
$$K_{u,v}(y,dx)=\frac{p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)}{p_{T-u}(y)}dx.$$
Consequently $Y$ solves the local martingale problem for $D_{T-u}$ in its natural reversed filtration. The occupation condition is an explicit hypothesis of this intermediate lemma; its applicability must be proved, not inferred from density notation.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a real continuous local martingale on $[0,T]$ with $M_0=0$, where a local martingale means that some increasing stopping times tending to $T$ make the stopped processes martingales. Then there is a unique continuous increasing process $[M]$ with $[M]_0=0$ such that the step-endpoint and partial-increment sums of squared increments along every deterministic partition sequence whose mesh tends to zero converge uniformly in probability to $[M]$. Moreover $M_t^2-[M]_t$ is a continuous local martingale. For a continuous $d$-dimensional local martingale $M$ started at zero, polarization defines continuous covariations $[M^i,M^j]$ with $M^iM^j-[M^i,M^j]$ local martingales. More generally, if $X=M+A$ and $Z=N+C$ with continuous local martingales $M,N$ and continuous finite-variation processes $A,C$, then left-step sums define the localized integrals against $M,N$ and
$$X_tZ_t-X_0Z_0=\int_0^t X_s\,dZ_s+\int_0^t Z_s\,dX_s+[M,N]_t,$$
where finite-variation integrals are pathwise Lebesgue–Stieltjes integrals and local-martingale integrals are the limits of the displayed left-step sums. Stopping a continuous local martingale at a bounded stopping time preserves its local-martingale property; if the stopped process is bounded, it is a true martingale. A continuous finite-variation local martingale is constant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a finite horizon $T>0$ and a filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$. Let $M$ be a continuous adapted $d$-dimensional local martingale with $M_0=0$. Let $\sigma$ be a predictable process of invertible $d\times d$ matrices, with $\|\sigma_t^{-1}\|\le C$ for a finite deterministic constant $C$ and $\int_0^T\|\sigma_t\|_F^2dt<\infty$ almost surely. Suppose
$$[M^i,M^j]_t=\int_0^t(\sigma_s\sigma_s^{\mathsf T})_{ij}ds.$$
Then predictable elementary sums, completed in the localized bracket-energy norm, define $B=\int\sigma^{-1}dM$. It has an adapted continuous version, is standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion in the given filtration, and
$$M_t=\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s$$
up to indistinguishability. The integral on the right is the localized predictable Brownian integral defined by elementary sums and their $L^2$ completion. This construction on the given finite horizon does not require completeness or right continuity of the filtration, and no continuity of $\sigma$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Assume AC. On a usual filtered probability space let $W$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion relative to that filtration: $W$ is adapted, and $W_t-W_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ with law $N(0,(t-s)I_m)$ for $s<t$. Let
$$Z_t=Z_0+\int_0^t\beta_sds+\int_0^t\Sigma_sdW_s,\qquad 0\le t\le T<\infty,$$
be a continuous $\mathbb R^d$-valued Itô process, with finite $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $Z_0$, progressively measurable $\beta$ and predictable $\Sigma$, and $\int_0^T(|\beta_s|+\|\Sigma_s\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2)ds<\infty$ almost surely. Suppose $a_s=\tfrac12\Sigma_s\Sigma_s^{\mathsf T}\ge\kappa I$ for $dt\otimes P$-almost every $(s,\omega)$, for a constant $\kappa>0$. For every stopping time $\gamma\le T$ with
$$E\int_0^\gamma(|\beta_s|+\operatorname{tr}a_s)ds<\infty,$$
the finite Borel measure $\mu_\gamma(E)=E\int_0^\gamma1_E(s,Z_s)ds$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $(d+1)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. In particular there are stopping times $\gamma_n\uparrow T$ almost surely with this property. No moment assumption on $Z_0$ is required.

derivations.claim: For $u<v$, the joint density of $(X_{T-v},X_{T-u})$ is $p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)$. Dividing by the strictly positive later marginal $p_{T-u}(y)$ gives the conditional law of $X_{T-v}$ given $X_{T-u}=y$, exactly $K_{u,v}(y,dx)$. Its normalization and reverse Chapman–Kolmogorov identity follow from [F1], so $Y$ is Markov with those transitions.

Choose an auxiliary nonexplosive continuous solution $Z$ of the assumed reverse martingale problem, with initial density $p_T$. Compact coordinate cutoffs give $Z=Z_0+\int\widetilde b\,du+N$ locally in state, with $N$ a continuous local martingale. Coordinate-product cutoffs and [F4] identify $[N]_u=\int_0^u a_{T-v}(Z_v)dv$: subtract the two product compensators and use that a continuous finite-variation local martingale is constant. The compact-test integrals make the local drift and trace integrals finite; nonexplosion and continuity exhaust the finite interval, without a bound on $Z_0$. Work in the usual augmentation, which preserves these continuous local martingales by the stopped event-test argument in the proof of [F5]. Left-step approximations as in [F6] give a predictable version of $\sigma_{T-u}(Z_u)$, and [F5] constructs the auxiliary Brownian Itô representation with the same drift and bracket. If $C=\sup\|\sigma^{-1}\|$, then $a\ge C^{-2}I$. Stop when $|Z|$ or the accumulated drift-plus-trace energy reaches $n$; the stops exhaust $T$ and the expected stopped variation and trace are finite. Thus [F7] supplies their occupation absolute continuity. Apply [F2], using only the original classical forward equations for $q,p$ and the actual forward path continuity: it identifies all marginals and Bayes kernels of $Z$ with those of $Y$, and transfers the compact-test local martingale problem to $Y$ in its natural reversed filtration. In particular the displayed operator is its extended martingale generator.

Fix $R$ and stop when $|Y|$ first reaches $R$. Compactly supported cutoffs equal to $x_i$ and $x_ix_j$ on the ball of radius $R$ turn the compact-test martingale identities into coordinate and coordinate-product identities. Subtracting the finite-variation drift in each coordinate identity gives continuous local martingales $M^i$. The product formula in [F4] shows that $Y_iY_j-Y_i(0)Y_j(0)-\int_0^{\cdot}(\widetilde b_iY_j+\widetilde b_jY_i)dr-[M_i,M_j]$ is a local martingale. The coordinate-product test shows that the same expression with $\int_0^{\cdot}a_{ij}(T-r,Y_r)dr$ in place of $[M_i,M_j]$ is a local martingale. Their difference is a continuous finite-variation local martingale, hence constant by [F4]; it starts at zero. Thus $[M_i,M_j]_u=\int_0^u a_{ij}(T-r,Y_r)dr$. Letting $R\uparrow\infty$ is valid because the assumed solution is nonexplosive.

To handle the Borel coefficients allowed by the SDE data, choose the predictable representative $\widehat Y$ obtained as follows: take left-step approximations with coefficients $Y_{kT/2^n}$, set their time-zero value to $Y_0$, and take their pointwise limit where finite and $0$ otherwise. These maps are predictable by [F6] and agree with $Y$ at every time on its common continuity event. The pair $(r,\widehat Y_r)$ is predictable, so the joint Borel coefficient gives a predictable matrix $\Sigma_r=\sigma_{T-r}(\widehat Y_r)$; inversion is Borel on invertible matrices, and $\|\Sigma_r^{-1}\|$ is uniformly bounded. Step 3.2 gives $\int_0^T\|\Sigma_r\|_F^2dr=\operatorname{tr}[M]_T<\infty$ almost surely, as well as $[M]_u=\int_0^u\Sigma_r\Sigma_r^{\mathsf T}dr$. Thus [F5] constructs $B=\int\Sigma^{-1}dM$ Brownian in the original reversed filtration, and proves $M=\int\Sigma\,dB$. Since $\widehat Y=Y$ on a common full event, this is the displayed reverse SDE with its original Borel coefficient. The assumed well-posedness and nonexplosion of the reverse martingale problem identify its law uniquely and complete the theorem.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in the closed ball $\overline B(0,R)$ for some finite $R\ge0$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, and set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, take $X_0$ with law $\mu$, measurable at time zero and independent of the future Brownian increments. Let $W$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to the filtration, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$ for every $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X$ be the strong solution of $dX_t=g(t)\,dW_t$ with initial value $X_0$. For $a>0$ define the product Gaussian density $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. For $t>0$ and $0\le s<t\le T$, define

$$p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz),\qquad q(s,x;t,y)=\phi_{v(t)-v(s)}(y-x).$$

Then $p_t$ is a finite, strictly positive, normalized Lebesgue density of the law of $X_t$. For each $x$, $q(s,x;t,\cdot)$ is a finite, strictly positive, normalized Lebesgue density, and for all Borel sets $A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$,

$$P(X_s\in A,\ X_t\in B)=\int_A\int_B q(s,x;t,y)\,dy\,\mu_s(dx),\qquad \mu_s:=\operatorname{Law}(X_s).$$

For $0\le s<r<t\le T$, these transition densities satisfy

$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}q(s,x;r,z)q(r,z;t,y)\,dz=q(s,x;t,y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^d).$$

No Lebesgue density for the initial law $\mu$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $d\ge1$, $T>0$, a finite $R\ge0$, and a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in $\overline B(0,R)$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, and set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, let $X_0$ be measurable at time zero with law $\mu$ and independent of future Brownian increments. Let $W$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to the filtration, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ for every $s<t$, and let $X$ be the unique strong solution of $X_t=X_0+\int_0^t g(r)\,dW_r$. For $a>0$ define $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. For $t>0$ set

$$p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz),$$

and set $\mu_0=\mu$. Let $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ denote the real infinitely differentiable functions with compact support. For every $t>0$, $p_t$ is positive and infinitely differentiable in $x$. On each interval $[\epsilon,T]$ with $0<\epsilon<T$, it is continuously differentiable in time and satisfies

$$\partial_t p_t(x)=\frac{g(t)^2}{2}\Delta_xp_t(x),\qquad \Delta_x=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}^2.$$

A family $(\nu_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ of Borel probability measures is narrowly continuous when $t\mapsto\int f\,d\nu_t$ is continuous for every bounded continuous real function $f$. It is a weak forward solution with initial law $\mu$ when it is narrowly continuous, $\nu_0=\mu$, and, for every $t\in[0,T]$ and every real-valued function $\psi:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with continuous first time derivative and continuous spatial derivatives through order two, whose spatial support lies in one compact set for all $s$, it satisfies

$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\psi(t,x)\,\nu_t(dx)-\int_{\mathbb R^d}\psi(0,x)\,\mu(dx)=\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R^d}\left(\partial_s\psi(s,x)+\frac{g(s)^2}{2}\Delta_x\psi(s,x)\right)\nu_s(dx)\,ds.$$

Then $(\mu_t)_{0\le t\le T}$, where $\mu_t(dx)=p_t(x)\,dx$ for $t>0$ and $\mu_0=\mu$, is the unique narrowly continuous weak forward solution with initial law $\mu$. No density for $\mu$ at $t=0$ is asserted.

For $a>0$, define the product Gaussian density $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. The operator norm below is induced by the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^d$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the hypotheses of the compactly supported Gaussian smoothing setup: $d\ge1$, $T>0$, $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure supported in $\overline B(0,R)$ for finite $R\ge0$, $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ is continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$, and $p_t(x)=\int\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz)$ for $t>0$. Fix $0<\epsilon<T$. For $t\in[\epsilon,T]$ and $x\in\mathbb R^d$, define the probability measure

$$\nu_{t,x}(dz)=\frac{\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)}{p_t(x)}\,\mu(dz),\qquad m_{t,x}=\int z\,\nu_{t,x}(dz),$$

and the matrix

$$C_{t,x}=\int (z-m_{t,x})(z-m_{t,x})^{\mathsf T}\,\nu_{t,x}(dz).$$

The density $p_t$ is positive and smooth, and its score $s_t(x):=\nabla_x\log p_t(x)$ satisfies

$$s_t(x)=-\frac{x-m_{t,x}}{v(t)},\qquad D_xs_t(x)=-\frac{I_d}{v(t)}+\frac{C_{t,x}}{v(t)^2}.$$

For all $t\in[\epsilon,T]$ and $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,

$$\|D_xs_t(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\frac1{v(\epsilon)}+\frac{R^2}{v(\epsilon)^2},\qquad |s_t(x)|\le\frac{|x|+R}{v(\epsilon)},$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For $a>0$ define $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. For $t>0$ set

$$p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz),$$

and set $\mu_0=\mu$. Let $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ denote the real infinitely differentiable functions with compact support. For every $t>0$, $p_t$ is positive and infinitely differentiable in $x$. On each interval $[\epsilon,T]$ with $0<\epsilon<T$, it is continuously differentiable in time and satisfies

$$\partial_t p_t(x)=\frac{g(t)^2}{2}\Delta_xp_t(x),\qquad \Delta_x=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}^2.$$

Set $K_{u,u}(y,\cdot)=\delta_y$. These are the Bayes-reversed kernels of the additive Gaussian smoothing process, including the posterior kernel at the original data time; no density for $\mu$ is required.

$$\widetilde L_u\varphi(y)=g(T-u)^2\left(s_{T-u}(y)\cdot\nabla\varphi(y)+\tfrac12\Delta\varphi(y)\right),\qquad \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d).$$
Then $Y$ is Markov with those reversed kernels, and for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty$ the process
$$\varphi(Y_v)-\varphi(Y_0)-\int_0^v\widetilde L_r\varphi(Y_r)\,dr,\qquad 0\le v\le T-\epsilon,$$

$$\nu_{t,x}(dz)=\frac{\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)}{p_t(x)}\,\mu(dz),\qquad m_{t,x}=\int z\,\nu_{t,x}(dz),$$

$$C_{t,x}=\int (z-m_{t,x})(z-m_{t,x})^{\mathsf T}\,\nu_{t,x}(dz).$$

$$s_t(x)=-\frac{x-m_{t,x}}{v(t)},\qquad D_xs_t(x)=-\frac{I_d}{v(t)}+\frac{C_{t,x}}{v(t)^2}.$$

For all $t\in[\epsilon,T]$ and $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,

so $s_t$ is globally Lipschitz in $x$, uniformly over this truncated time interval, with Lipschitz constant at most $1/v(\epsilon)+R^2/v(\epsilon)^2$. No such bound is asserted uniformly as $\epsilon\downarrow0$.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a real continuous local martingale on $[0,T]$ with $M_0=0$, where a local martingale means that some increasing stopping times tending to $T$ make the stopped processes martingales. Then there is a unique continuous increasing process $[M]$ with $[M]_0=0$ such that the step-endpoint and partial-increment sums of squared increments along every deterministic partition sequence whose mesh tends to zero converge uniformly in probability to $[M]$. Moreover $M_t^2-[M]_t$ is a continuous local martingale. For a continuous $d$-dimensional local martingale $M$ started at zero, polarization defines continuous covariations $[M^i,M^j]$ with $M^iM^j-[M^i,M^j]$ local martingales. More generally, if $X=M+A$ and $Z=N+C$ with continuous local martingales $M,N$ and continuous finite-variation processes $A,C$, then left-step sums define the localized integrals against $M,N$ and
$$X_tZ_t-X_0Z_0=\int_0^t X_s\,dZ_s+\int_0^t Z_s\,dX_s+[M,N]_t,$$
where finite-variation integrals are pathwise Lebesgue–Stieltjes integrals and local-martingale integrals are the limits of the displayed left-step sums. Stopping a continuous local martingale at a bounded stopping time preserves its local-martingale property; if the stopped process is bounded, it is a true martingale. A continuous finite-variation local martingale is constant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(M_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a continuous adapted $d$-dimensional local martingale with $M_0=0$. Let $(\sigma_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a continuous adapted process of invertible $d\times d$ matrices such that $\|\sigma_t^{-1}\|\le C$ for a deterministic finite constant $C$, and suppose every entry of $\sigma$ is locally square-integrable in time almost surely. Write $[M^i,M^j]$ for the continuous bracket characterized by the local-martingale property of $M^iM^j-[M^i,M^j]$, and assume
$$[M^i,M^j]_t=\int_0^t(\sigma_s\sigma_s^{\mathsf T})_{ij}\,ds\qquad(1\le i,j\le d).$$
Then the stochastic integral $B_t=\int_0^t\sigma_s^{-1}\,dM_s$, constructed as the localized $L^2$ limit of left-step sums, has a continuous version with $[B^i,B^j]_t=\delta_{ij}t$. Consequently $B$ is a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion relative to the given filtration.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in $\overline B(0,R)$ for some finite $R\ge0$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable and satisfy $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$; set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, let $X_0$ be measurable at time zero with law $\mu$ and independent of future Brownian increments. Let $W$ be a standard adapted $d$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increment $W_t-W_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and has law $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$ for $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X$ be the unique strong solution of $X_t=X_0+\int_0^t g(r)\,dW_r$, and write $\mu_t=\operatorname{Law}(X_t)$. For Borel probability laws $\alpha,\beta$ with finite second moments, write $W_2(\alpha,\beta)$ for the square root of the infimum of $\int|x-y|^2\,d\pi(x,y)$ over Borel probability couplings $\pi$ of $\alpha$ and $\beta$. For every $0<\epsilon\le T$,

$$\mathbb E|X_\epsilon-X_0|^2=d\,v(\epsilon),\qquad W_2(\mu_\epsilon,\mu)\le\sqrt{d\,v(\epsilon)}.$$

right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in

$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ for $0\le s<t\le T$. Let

derivations.claim: By [F1], the reversed Gaussian kernels are normalized and compose, and [F2] gives the reverse martingale problem for $Y_u=X_{T-u}$ on $0\le u\le T-\epsilon$. In particular the reverse generator has drift $\beta_u(x)=g(T-u)^2\nabla\log p_{T-u}(x)$ and diffusion matrix $a_u(x)=g(T-u)^2I_d$.

Fix $R_1$ and stop when $|Y|$ reaches $R_1$. Compactly supported cutoffs equal to $x_i$ and $x_ix_j$ on that ball turn the identities in [F2] into coordinate and coordinate-product martingales. Subtracting the finite-variation drift gives continuous local martingales $M^i$. The product formula in [F4] makes $Y_iY_j-Y_i(0)Y_j(0)-\int(\beta_iY_j+\beta_jY_i)dr-[M_i,M_j]$ a local martingale. The coordinate-product identity makes the same expression with $\int g(T-r)^2\delta_{ij}dr$ in place of $[M_i,M_j]$ a local martingale. Their difference is a continuous finite-variation local martingale, hence constant by [F4]; it starts at zero. Thus $[M]_u=\int_0^u g(T-r)^2I_d dr$. Letting $R_1\uparrow\infty$ is valid because $Y$ has continuous paths on the compact time interval.

The process $\sigma_r=g(T-r)I_d$ is invertible with bounded inverse. Apply the inverse-diffusion construction in [F4] to define $B_u=\int_0^u g(T-r)^{-1}dM_r$. Thus $B$ remains Brownian in the usual augmentation. The decomposition of $M$ gives the displayed reverse SDE.

By [F3], $\beta_u$ is globally Lipschitz in $x$ uniformly on the truncated interval, with constant at most $g_{\max}^2(1/v(\epsilon)+R^2/v(\epsilon)^2)$; its linear-growth bound follows by multiplying the supplied score bound by $g_{\max}^2$. The diffusion coefficient $g(T-u)I_d$ is deterministic and bounded. The initial value $Y_0=X_T$ has finite second moment since $X_0$ is bounded and the Gaussian increment has finite second moment. Thus [F6] gives a unique strong solution for the same initial value and Brownian motion $B$ on the usual augmented reversed filtration. Pathwise uniqueness identifies this solution with the weak solution $Y$ from step 3.1.

Since $Y_{T-\epsilon}=X_\epsilon$, the endpoint coupling statement [F5] gives the exact mean-square error and $W_2$ bound. Because $v(\epsilon)\le g_{\max}^2\epsilon\to0$, the coupling proves $L^2$ convergence to $X_0$; the same supplier gives weak convergence of the laws to $\mu$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $X_t$ have continuous paths on $[0,T]$ and be Markov on $\mathbb R^d$, meaning its conditional future law given the past depends only on its current state; nonexplosive means it remains in $\mathbb R^d$ throughout this finite interval. Let it have forward generator
$$L_t\phi=b_t\cdot\nabla\phi+\tfrac12a_t:D^2\phi,$$
where $a_t=\sigma_t\sigma_t^{\mathsf T}$ is symmetric and $L_t^*r=-\partial_i(b_{t,i}r)+\tfrac12\partial_i\partial_j(a_{t,ij}r)$. Assume positive $C^{1,2}$ marginal densities $p_t$ and positive transition densities $q(s,x;t,y)$ satisfy the marginal identity and Chapman–Kolmogorov identity, and that $\partial_t p_t=L_t^*p_t$ and $\partial_tq(s,x;t,y)=L_t^{*,y}q(s,x;t,y)$ hold classically. Assume for every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ that the transition-density integrals can be differentiated in time, the resulting derivatives are integrable, and integration by parts in the state variable has no boundary term.

Define $K_{u,v}$ by the Bayes-reversed kernel formula for $0\le u\le v\le T$. Then the reversed process $Y_u=X_{T-u}$ is Markov with transitions $K_{u,v}$. For compact smooth $\phi$, define the formal adjoint candidate operator
$$\widetilde L_u\phi(y)=\frac{L_{T-u}^*(p_{T-u}\phi)(y)-\phi(y)L_{T-u}^*p_{T-u}(y)}{p_{T-u}(y)}.$$
The product rule gives the identity
$$\widetilde L_u\phi=\widetilde b_u\cdot\nabla\phi+\tfrac12a_{T-u}:D^2\phi,\qquad \widetilde b_u=-b_{T-u}+\nabla\!\cdot a_{T-u}+a_{T-u}\nabla\log p_{T-u},$$
with $(\nabla\!\cdot a)_i=\sum_j\partial_j a_{ij}$. These Bayes-kernel and formal product identities use only the preceding hypotheses.

For the martingale conclusion, impose additionally the following forward analytic conditions. For every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^d$, with $A_{ij}(r,x)=p_r(x)a_{r,ij}(x)$ and $C_i=-p_rb_{r,i}+\sum_j\partial_jA_{ij}$,
$$\int_0^T\!\int_K\left[\sum_i|C_i|+\sum_{i,j}p_r|a_{r,ij}|\right]dx\,dr<\infty.$$
For every $t\in(0,T]$ and $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, the actual forward conditional expectation $g_{t,f}(r,x)=\int q(r,x;t,y)f(y)dy$ has a $C^{1,2}$ version on $(0,t)\times\mathbb R^d$, solves $\partial_rg_{t,f}+L_rg_{t,f}=0$, and satisfies $\int p_r\phi L_rg_{t,f}dx=\int g_{t,f}L_r^*(p_r\phi)dx$ for each compact smooth $\phi$ and almost every $r<t$. All coefficient expressions in these conditions are Borel. These are conditions on the original forward transition family.

Under these additional forward analytic conditions, $\widetilde L_u$ is the extended martingale generator of $Y$: for its natural reversed filtration $\mathcal G_u=\sigma(Y_r:0\le r\le u)$, every compact-test compensated process is a martingale, hence a local martingale. The unconditional formal candidate identity alone makes no martingale or pointwise transition-quotient assertion.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].
Assume AC. The function $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ is positive and Borel measurable on $\mathbb R$, with Lebesgue integral one.

derivations.claim: Define $\displaystyle \psi(y)=\begin{cases}\exp\!\left(-\frac1{1-y^2}\right),&|y|<1,\\0,&|y|\ge1.\end{cases}$ Every derivative extends continuously by zero at $y=\pm1$ because $u^{-m}e^{-1/u}\to0$ as $u\downarrow0$ for every integer $m\ge0$; hence $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$. Its first and second derivatives are bounded, and $\psi''$ is not identically zero, since a compactly supported function with zero second derivative would be affine and therefore zero. Choose $\alpha>0$ with $\alpha\|\psi'\|_\infty<1/2$ and set $h(y)=y+\alpha\psi(y)$. Then $h'(y)=1+\alpha\psi'(y)>1/2$, $h$ equals the identity outside $[-1,1]$, and it is strictly increasing and onto; the inverse function theorem makes it a smooth diffeomorphism.

Set $X_t=h(W_t)$ and $z=h^{-1}(x)$. By Itô's formula [F1], $\displaystyle dX_t=b(X_t)dt+\sigma(X_t)dW_t,\qquad b(x)=\tfrac12h''(h^{-1}(x)),\quad \sigma(x)=h'(h^{-1}(x)).$ Because $h'$ is bounded below by $1/2$, and $h''$ and $h'''$ are bounded and vanish outside a compact set, both $b$ and $\sigma$ are globally Lipschitz and bounded. Thus this diffusion is nonexplosive and uniformly elliptic, with $a(x)=\sigma(x)^2$.

For $t>0$, $W_t$ has density $\phi_t$ by [F5], and the change-of-variables formula [F2] gives $\displaystyle p_t(x)=\frac{\phi_t(h^{-1}(x))}{h'(h^{-1}(x))}.$ Likewise, for $0\le s<t$ its transition density is $\displaystyle q(s,x;t,y)=\frac{\phi_{t-s}(h^{-1}(y)-h^{-1}(x))}{h'(h^{-1}(y))}.$ These densities are positive and smooth. They satisfy the marginal and Chapman–Kolmogorov identities because they are the images under $h$ of Brownian marginal and transition laws.

Write $z=h^{-1}(x)$. Differentiating $a(x)=h'(z)^2$ and using $dz/dx=1/h'(z)$ gives $\displaystyle a'(x)=2h'(z)h''(z)\frac1{h'(z)}=2h''(z).$ Since $h''=\alpha\psi''$ is nonzero at some $y_*$, $a'(h(y_*))\ne0$.

Fix $0<\epsilon<T$ and reindex the actual process on $[\epsilon,T]$ as $\bar X_s=X_{\epsilon+s}$ on $[0,T-\epsilon]$. Write $\bar p_s=p_{\epsilon+s}$ and $\bar q(r,x;s,y)=q(\epsilon+r,x;\epsilon+s,y)$. The explicit formulas in step 3.1 are positive and smooth on this shifted interval, satisfy the marginal and Chapman–Kolmogorov identities because they are images of Brownian transition laws under the diffeomorphism $h$, and solve the forward density equations for the coefficients in step 2.1 by direct differentiation and the chain rule. Since $h$ equals the identity outside a compact set, these densities and their differentiated integrands have Gaussian tails; differentiation under transition integrals is absolutely integrable and integration by parts has no boundary term. The new forward analytic conditions can also be checked directly: for $f\in C_c^\infty$, put $F=f\circ h$ and $z=h^{-1}(x)$. Then $F\in C_c^\infty$ and $g_{t,f}(r,x)=\int\phi_{t-r}(w-z)F(w)dw$. Differentiation of the Gaussian convolution, followed by two integrations by parts against $F$, gives $\partial_rg_{t,f}=-L_rg_{t,f}$ and $|L_rg_{t,f}|\le\tfrac12\|F''\|_\infty$; the chain rule gives $L_rg=\tfrac12\partial_{zz}(g\circ h)$. The densities and all weighted coefficients $p b$, $p a$, and $\partial_x(pa)$ are jointly bounded on compact subsets of $[\epsilon,T]\times\mathbb R$, so the displayed local weighted integrals are finite; the spatial adjoint identity follows by compact-support integration by parts. The process is continuous, nonexplosive and Markov. Introduce reverse time $u\in[0,T-\epsilon]$ and $Y_u=\bar X_{T-\epsilon-u}=X_{T-u}$. The local generator lemma applies to this actual reversed process and gives drift $\displaystyle \widetilde b_u(x)=-b(x)+a'(x)+a(x)\partial_x\log p_{T-u}(x).$ For $|x|\ge1$, $h^{-1}(x)=x$, $h'(x)=1$, $h''(x)=0$, and $p_t(x)=\phi_t(x)$, so this drift is $-x/(T-u)$. On $|x|\le1$ it is smooth with bounded state derivative uniformly for $u\in[0,T-\epsilon]$, because $p_t$ has a positive minimum there. Thus $\widetilde b$ is globally Lipschitz with linear growth on the truncated interval; the reverse diffusion coefficient $\sigma$ is bounded, globally Lipschitz, and bounded away from zero.

At $x_*=h(y_*)$, the actual reverse generator from [F3] has drift differing from the score-only expression $-b+a\partial_x\log p_t$ by the nonzero amount $a'(x_*)$. By continuity, the drift difference remains nonzero on an open interval about $x_*$, and the reversed marginal density is positive there. Thus the score-only coefficient is not the actual reverse generator on a set of positive reversed probability. This refutes the claim.

Assume AC. Fix $t_0<T$, integers $d,r\ge1$, and a filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t_0\le t\le T},P)$ satisfying the usual conditions. Let $W$ be an adapted standard $r$-dimensional Brownian motion such that $W_t-W_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and has law $N_r(0,(t-s)I_r)$ for every $t_0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X_{t_0}$ be $\mathcal F_{t_0}$-measurable, almost surely bounded, and independent of the future Brownian increments $\sigma(W_t-W_{t_0}:t_0\le t\le T)$. Let
$$dX_t=b(X_t,t)\,dt+\sigma(X_t,t)\,dW_t,\qquad X_t\in\mathbb R^d,$$
for $t\in[t_0,T]$. Assume the drift and diffusion path integrals satisfy $\int_{t_0}^T|b(X_s,s)|ds<\infty$ and $\int_{t_0}^T\|\sigma(X_s,s)\|_F^2ds<\infty$ almost surely, and that this SDE has a unique nonexplosive strong solution. Put $a=\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T}$. Also assume the strong restart property: for each deterministic $s\in[t_0,T]$, the future path $(X_r)_{s\le r\le T}$ is almost surely a measurable function of $X_s$ and $(W_r-W_s)_{s\le r\le T}$. Assume the coefficients and densities are smooth enough for the displayed derivatives and Itô identities to hold. Assume the marginal density $p_t(x)$ is positive wherever used and is a unique smooth solution of
$$\partial_t p_t=L_t^*p_t,\qquad L_t^*r=-\sum_i\partial_i(b_i r)+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\partial_i\partial_j(a_{ij}r).$$
Define the $r$-vector process $\widetilde W$ by $\widetilde W_{t_0}=0$ and
$$d\widetilde W_t^k=dW_t^k+c_k(X_t,t)\,dt,\qquad c_k(x,t)=p_t(x)^{-1}\sum_i\partial_i\!\left(p_t(x)\sigma_{ik}(x,t)\right).$$
Assume the augmented process $(X,\widetilde W)$ has a unique smooth joint density solving its augmented forward Kolmogorov equation for $t>t_0$, and for every $t>s\ge t_0$ its conditional joint density given $\widetilde W_s$ is the unique smooth solution of the corresponding conditional augmented equation; all displayed derivatives and density integrals are valid. Then the following hold.

1. For $t>s\ge t_0$, $X_t$ is independent of $\widetilde W_t-\widetilde W_s$, and this increment has law $N_r(0,(t-s)I_r)$.
2. Put $U=T-t_0$, $Y_u=X_{T-u}$, and $B_u=\widetilde W_{T-u}-\widetilde W_T$ for $0\le u\le U$. With $\mathcal G_u=\sigma(Y_v,B_v:0\le v\le u)$, $B$ is a standard $r$-dimensional Brownian motion relative to $(\mathcal G_u)$.
3. In the backward Itô convention, $Y$ satisfies
$$dY_u=\left[-b(Y_u,T-u)+(\nabla\!\cdot a)(Y_u,T-u)+a(Y_u,T-u)\nabla\log p_{T-u}(Y_u)\right]du+\sigma(Y_u,T-u)\,dB_u,$$
where $(\nabla\!\cdot a)_i=\sum_j\partial_j a_{ij}$. The score is asserted only where $p_{T-u}>0$; no density or score regularity beyond the stated hypotheses is implied.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in the closed ball $\overline B(0,R)$ for some finite $R\ge0$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, and set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, take $X_0$ with law $\mu$, measurable at time zero and independent of the future Brownian increments. Let $W$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to the filtration, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$ for every $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X$ be the strong solution of $dX_t=g(t)\,dW_t$ with initial value $X_0$. For $a>0$ define the product Gaussian density $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. For $t>0$ and $0\le s<t\le T$, define

$$p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz),\qquad q(s,x;t,y)=\phi_{v(t)-v(s)}(y-x).$$

Then $p_t$ is a finite, strictly positive, normalized Lebesgue density of the law of $X_t$. For each $x$, $q(s,x;t,\cdot)$ is a finite, strictly positive, normalized Lebesgue density, and for all Borel sets $A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$,

$$P(X_s\in A,\ X_t\in B)=\int_A\int_B q(s,x;t,y)\,dy\,\mu_s(dx),\qquad \mu_s:=\operatorname{Law}(X_s).$$

For $0\le s<r<t\le T$, these transition densities satisfy

$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}q(s,x;r,z)q(r,z;t,y)\,dz=q(s,x;t,y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^d).$$

No Lebesgue density for the initial law $\mu$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $d\ge1$, $T>0$, a finite $R\ge0$, and a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in $\overline B(0,R)$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, and set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, let $X_0$ be measurable at time zero with law $\mu$ and independent of future Brownian increments. Let $W$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to the filtration, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ for every $s<t$, and let $X$ be the unique strong solution of $X_t=X_0+\int_0^t g(r)\,dW_r$. For $a>0$ define $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. For $t>0$ set

$$p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz),$$

and set $\mu_0=\mu$. Let $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ denote the real infinitely differentiable functions with compact support. For every $t>0$, $p_t$ is positive and infinitely differentiable in $x$. On each interval $[\epsilon,T]$ with $0<\epsilon<T$, it is continuously differentiable in time and satisfies

$$\partial_t p_t(x)=\frac{g(t)^2}{2}\Delta_xp_t(x),\qquad \Delta_x=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}^2.$$

A family $(\nu_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ of Borel probability measures is narrowly continuous when $t\mapsto\int f\,d\nu_t$ is continuous for every bounded continuous real function $f$. It is a weak forward solution with initial law $\mu$ when it is narrowly continuous, $\nu_0=\mu$, and, for every $t\in[0,T]$ and every real-valued function $\psi:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with continuous first time derivative and continuous spatial derivatives through order two, whose spatial support lies in one compact set for all $s$, it satisfies

$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\psi(t,x)\,\nu_t(dx)-\int_{\mathbb R^d}\psi(0,x)\,\mu(dx)=\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R^d}\left(\partial_s\psi(s,x)+\frac{g(s)^2}{2}\Delta_x\psi(s,x)\right)\nu_s(dx)\,ds.$$

Then $(\mu_t)_{0\le t\le T}$, where $\mu_t(dx)=p_t(x)\,dx$ for $t>0$ and $\mu_0=\mu$, is the unique narrowly continuous weak forward solution with initial law $\mu$. No density for $\mu$ at $t=0$ is asserted.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a finite integer $d\ge1$, a horizon $T>0$, and a complete filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T},P)$. Let $W=(W_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to the filtration, and assume that for every $0\le s<t\le T$ the vector increment $W_t-W_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and has law $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with constants $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$, and define $M_t=(\int_0^t g(r)\,dW_r^1,\ldots,\int_0^t g(r)\,dW_r^d)$ by coordinatewise scalar Itô integration. For every $0\le s<t\le T$, the increment $M_t-M_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and has law $N_d(0,(v(t)-v(s))I_d)$. Consequently, the increments of $M$ over every finite increasing time list are mutually independent.

For real $a,b,t$, $\varphi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\varphi_X(at)$. For a finite mutually independent family $(X_j)_{j=1}^n$ of real random variables, $\varphi_{\sum_jX_j}(t)=\prod_j\varphi_{X_j}(t)$. The empty sum has characteristic function one.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice as required by the stochastic-integral interfaces
below. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ and finite integers $d,m\ge1$. Work on
a complete filtered probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T},P)$ whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$ (the usual conditions).

Let $W=(W_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] adapted to this filtration, with
$W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ for $0\le s<t\le T$. Let
$X_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, satisfy
$E|X_0|^2<\infty$, and be independent of the future Brownian increments.
Explicitly, $X_0$ is independent of the sigma-algebra
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$.

Continuity of a process means continuity on one measurable event of
probability one. We use an everywhere-continuous adapted representative: if
the chosen process is continuous only on such an event $A$, replace it off $A$
by its initial value. Since $A^c$ is a null set and the filtration is complete,
$A^c\in\mathcal F_0$; the replacement preserves adaptedness and changes the
SDE identity only on a null event, hence preserves it up to
indistinguishability.

The drift and diffusion coefficients are jointly Borel maps
$$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d,\qquad \sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}.$$
For nonnegative finite constants $L,K$, assume for every $t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$ that
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|).$$
Here $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm and
$\|A\|_F^2=\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{k=1}^m|A^{ik}|^2$ is the Frobenius norm.

For an adapted continuous candidate $X:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$,
the vector Itô equation
$$X_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(s,X_s)\,ds+\left(\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}(s,X_s)\,dW_s^k\right)_{i=1}^d,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
uses a pathwise Lebesgue integral for the drift and, in each coordinate, the
localized Itô integral from
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], clause 2. Require
$\int_0^T|b(s,X_s)|ds<\infty$ and
$\int_0^T\|\sigma(s,X_s)\|_F^2ds<\infty$ almost surely; these are the local
coefficient-integrability conditions in that definition. When a coordinate
integrand has finite expected energy, its integral is the square-integrable
Itô integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]];
the Picard estimates below establish that stronger condition for every input
in $\mathcal H_T$. Equality of processes means
equality for every $t$ on one measurable event of probability one, that is,
indistinguishability
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. A **strong
solution on $[0,T]$** is an adapted continuous process satisfying this
integral equation indistinguishably. No moment bound is included in the
definition; the existence theorem proves its $L^2$ path-sup bound.
The usual-filtration, continuity, and finite-coordinate conventions agree
with the multidimensional class of continuous Brownian Itô processes
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. This definition makes no ellipticity,
transition-density, forward-equation, or time-reversal assertion.

Brownian motion here means the finite-horizon version of the cited definition:
$W_0=0$ almost surely, with continuous paths and the stated increments on
$[0,T]$. All cited stochastic-calculus interfaces are used on this interval.
Their constructions require no extension of $W$ beyond $T$: elementary
integrals use only increments between partition points in $[0,T]$, and their
$L^2$ limits and continuous versions are constructed on that same interval.
For a predictable scalar integrand $H$ with finite pathwise energy, localize
at $\rho_n=\inf\{t\in[0,T]:\int_0^t H_s^2ds\ge n\}\wedge T$.
Here $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$.
The stopped integrands have expected energy at most $n$; their continuous
integrals agree up to the smaller stop by the finite-energy stopping identity.
On the full event of finite energy, $\rho_n=T$ for all sufficiently large
$n$, so these integrals paste uniquely on the whole closed interval $[0,T]$,
exactly as in the localized construction of
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. At $T=0$ every integral is zero.

Assume the data and hypotheses of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] on $[0,T]$, with $T\ge0$, finite
dimensions $d,m\ge1$, Lipschitz constant $L$, and linear-growth constant
$K$. There is a strong solution $X$ on the given filtered probability space.
It is unique up to indistinguishability among strong solutions with the same
initial value and Brownian driver, and it satisfies
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t|^2\le(1+3E|X_0|^2)e^{C_TT},\qquad C_T:=6K^2T+24mK^2.$$
The bound is independent of any later numerical mesh.

Put $C=C([0,\infty),\mathbb R)$, give $C$ the uniform-on-compacts topology,
and write $\pi_t(f)=f(t)$. Then
$$\mathcal B(C)=\sigma(\pi_t:t\ge0)=\sigma(\pi_q:q\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,\infty)).$$
Here each expression on the right denotes the smallest sigma-algebra on $C$
making every displayed coordinate map measurable. No choice principle is used.
The finite-coordinate cylinders in $E=\prod_{i\in I}E_i$ form a pi-system.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

derivations.claim: Applying [F1] to $e^{\theta t}(X_t-\mu)$ gives, for $t\ge s$, $\displaystyle X_t-\mu=e^{-\theta(t-s)}(X_s-\mu)+\sigma\int_s^t e^{-\theta(t-r)}dW_r.$ The last term is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and by [F2] is centered normal with variance $\displaystyle \sigma^2\int_s^t e^{-2\theta(t-r)}dr=\frac{\sigma^2}{2\theta}\left(1-e^{-2\theta(t-s)}\right).$ With $q=\sigma^2/(2\theta)$ and $X_0-\mu\sim N(0,q)$, the mean of $X_t$ is $\mu$ and its variance is $e^{-2\theta t}q+q(1-e^{-2\theta t})=q$. Independence and Gaussian addition [F3, F4] therefore give the same marginal law at every $t$.

Fix $s<t$ and write $r=e^{-\theta(t-s)}$, $U=X_s-\mu$, and $V=X_t-\mu=rU+\eta$, where $U\sim N(0,q)$ and $\eta\sim N(0,q(1-r^2))$ is independent of $U$ by step 1.1. Their joint density is proportional to $\displaystyle \exp\!\left[-\frac12\left(\frac{u^2}{q}+\frac{(v-ru)^2}{q(1-r^2)}\right)\right],\qquad \frac{u^2}{q}+\frac{(v-ru)^2}{q(1-r^2)}=\frac{(u-rv)^2}{q(1-r^2)}+\frac{v^2}{q}.$ Thus $X_s\mid X_t=y$ has law $N(\mu+r(y-\mu),q(1-r^2))$, exactly the forward transition law over the same time gap. Bayes' formula shows that the reversed transition kernels equal the forward OU transition kernels.

By [F5] and step 2.1, the reversed process starts from the stationary law and has the same transition kernels as the forward OU process. Indeed, the forward joint density along an ordered time list is the stationary density times the product of the forward transition densities. The Bayes identity in step 2.1 gives detailed balance for each transition factor, so reversing this product gives the Markov factorization with the same kernels in reverse-time order. Thus all finite-dimensional distributions of $Y$ equal those of the forward OU process. Extend each path constantly after $T$; the extended paths are random elements of $C([0,\infty),\mathbb R)$ because each coordinate evaluation is measurable. By [F7], their Borel laws are equal. On a forward OU path define $\displaystyle \Gamma(X)_u=\frac{X_u-X_0+\theta\int_0^u(X_r-\mu)\,dr}{\sigma},\quad 0\le u\le T.$ The integral equation makes $\Gamma(X)=W$; because the natural filtration of $X$ is contained in the forward filtration, this driver is Brownian relative to that natural filtration. The map from a continuous path to $\Gamma(X)$ is continuous in the uniform norm on $[0,T]$, so equality of path laws transfers this Brownian property to $B_u:=\Gamma(Y)_u$. Rearranging its definition gives $dY_u=-\theta(Y_u-\mu)\,du+\sigma\,dB_u$ in the natural reversed filtration. Finally, the stationary score is $\partial_x\log p(x)=-(x-\mu)/q=-2\theta(x-\mu)/\sigma^2$. With $b(x)=-\theta(x-\mu)$ and $a(x)=\sigma^2$, the score-form drift equals $-b(x)+a(x)\partial_x\log p(x)=\theta(x-\mu)-2\theta(x-\mu)=-\theta(x-\mu)$, as stated.
