citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$ and let
$M=(M^1,\dots,M^d)$ be an adapted $\mathbb R^d$-valued process with continuous
paths such that every coordinate $M^i$ is a real continuous local martingale
relative to $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ in the sense of
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]]. Suppose $M_0=0$ almost surely and
whose quadratic covariations in the sense of
[[def-quadratic-covariation-of-brownian-ito-processes]] satisfy
$[M^i,M^j]_t=\delta_{ij}t$ for all $i,j$ and all $t\ge0$. Then $M$ is a
standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]],
and for all $0\le s<t$ the vector increment $M_t-M_s$ is independent of
$\mathcal F_s$ with law $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a real continuous local martingale on $[0,T]$ with $M_0=0$, where a local martingale means that some increasing stopping times tending to $T$ make the stopped processes martingales. Then there is a unique continuous increasing process $[M]$ with $[M]_0=0$ such that the step-endpoint and partial-increment sums of squared increments along every deterministic partition sequence whose mesh tends to zero converge uniformly in probability to $[M]$. Moreover $M_t^2-[M]_t$ is a continuous local martingale. For a continuous $d$-dimensional local martingale $M$ started at zero, polarization defines continuous covariations $[M^i,M^j]$ with $M^iM^j-[M^i,M^j]$ local martingales. More generally, if $X=M+A$ and $Z=N+C$ with continuous local martingales $M,N$ and continuous finite-variation processes $A,C$, then left-step sums define the localized integrals against $M,N$ and
$$X_tZ_t-X_0Z_0=\int_0^t X_s\,dZ_s+\int_0^t Z_s\,dX_s+[M,N]_t,$$
where finite-variation integrals are pathwise Lebesgue–Stieltjes integrals and local-martingale integrals are the limits of the displayed left-step sums. Stopping a continuous local martingale at a bounded stopping time preserves its local-martingale property; if the stopped process is bounded, it is a true martingale. A continuous finite-variation local martingale is constant.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
[[def-convergence-almost-everywhere-relative-to-a-measure]].

Assume AC. Let $N\in\mathbb N_0$, $p>1$, and $q=p/(p-1)$. If $X=(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ is a nonnegative submartingale and $X_N\in L^p$, then
$$\left\|\max_{0\le k\le N}X_k\right\|_p\le q\|X_N\|_p.$$
In particular, for a martingale $M$ with $M_N\in L^p$,
$$\left\|\max_{0\le k\le N}|M_k|\right\|_p\le q\|M_N\|_p.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The quotient is [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption is inherited from RN existence.

derivations.claim: First work in the completed right-continuous augmentation of the given filtration. This preserves every continuous local martingale used here. Indeed, each original stopped true martingale $Q$ is uniformly integrable on $[0,T]$, since $Q_s=E[Q_T\mid\mathcal F_s]$; the uniform integrability follows by truncating the fixed integrable terminal variable. If $s_k\downarrow s$, continuity and uniform integrability give $Q_{s_k}\to Q_s$ in $L^1$. For an event in the completed intersection of the $\mathcal F_{s_k}$, its martingale event identity with $Q_t$ therefore passes to $Q_s$; completion adds only null-event identities. This proves the martingale property in the augmented filtration, while original localizers remain stopping times there. Countably many continuous processes can now be normalized on their common null exceptional set in the initial sigma-algebra. Let $\tau_n$ be the first time $|M|$ or $A$ reaches $n$, capped at $T$. These are increasing stopping times equal to $T$ eventually on each path in the common full event of continuity and finite energy, with $M^{\tau_n}$ bounded and $A_{T\wedge\tau_n}\le n$; the latter processes are continuous, and their hitting times are stopping times by progressive measurability and the rational-time test for continuous paths. By the bounded-stopping result in [F2], the original localizers show that $M^{\tau_n}$ is a bounded local martingale. Dominated convergence in its localizing event-integral identities, including at terminal time $T$, makes it a true square-integrable martingale. Work first with one such stopped martingale $N=M^{\tau_n}$, bracket density $c_s=1_{s\le\tau_n}a_s$, and the finite measure $\mu(E)=E\int_0^T1_E(s,\omega)\operatorname{tr}(c_s)ds$ restricted to the original predictable sigma-algebra. All elementary approximants below are predictable for that original filtration; the stopped integrator $N$ is used in the augmented space.

Bounded elementary predictable functions are dense in $L^2(\mu)$. To see this without replacing $\mu$ by $dt\otimes P$, let $V$ be their $L^2(\mu)$ closure. Each interval-generator indicator belongs to $V$, and time-zero indicators have zero $\mu$ norm. The constant class is represented by $1_{(0,T]}$. The sets whose indicators belong to $V$ form a lambda-system: complements follow by subtraction from this constant class; for disjoint unions, finite partial sums converge in $L^2(\mu)$ because the squared tail norm is the tail measure and $\mu$ is finite. Intersections of generators are generators or empty, so [F3] makes every predictable-set indicator belong to $V$. Simple approximation, truncation and dominated convergence then give all of $L^2(\mu)$. Apply this entrywise for matrices.

For a bounded elementary matrix $G=\sum_kG_k1_{(t_k,t_{k+1}]}$ with $G_k$ measurable at $t_k$, define $I_N(G)_t=\sum_kG_k(N_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}-N_{t\wedge t_k})$. Conditional martingale-increment identities and [F2] give $$E|I_N(G)_T|^2=E\int_0^T\operatorname{tr}(G_sc_sG_s^{\mathsf T})ds,$$ and $I_N(G)^iI_N(G)^j-\int_0^{\cdot}(G_sc_sG_s^{\mathsf T})_{ij}ds$ is a martingale. The coordinate product-compensators of $N$ are true martingales: $N$ is bounded, and its bracket entries are bounded in absolute value by $A_{T\wedge\tau_n}\le n$, so the local martingales from [F2] are bounded and the preceding dominated-convergence argument applies. The displayed identities now follow on each block by multiplying those true martingale identities by bounded $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable coefficients, and then summing; cross-block increments have conditional mean zero. For elementary $G$, the integral is bounded by a deterministic multiple of the bound on $N$, and its compensator is bounded by a deterministic multiple of $n$, so these product-compensators are true martingales as well. For two elementary matrices apply the same isometry to their difference and [F4] to obtain the maximal bound with factor $4$. Since $c$ is positive semidefinite, its energy is bounded by $E\int\|G\|_F^2\operatorname{tr}(c)ds=\|G\|_{L^2(\mu)}^2$.

Thus for every predictable $J\in L^2(\mu)$, elementary approximants from step 1.2 have integrals converging in $L^2$ of the path supremum to $I_N(J)$. A subsequence with summable expected sup errors converges uniformly almost surely to a continuous version. Define its value at each time by the pointwise limit of this subsequence when finite, and zero otherwise; this is adapted and progressive and has continuous paths on the common full convergence event, without modifying a process on a potentially noninitial null event. Martingale event identities pass to the $L^1$ limit. Products converge in $L^1$ by Cauchy–Schwarz; the compensators converge in expected total variation by the same inequality in the energy inner product, since $\|J-G_m\|_{c}\to0$ and $\|G_m\|_c$ is bounded. Hence $$[I_N(J)]_t=\int_0^tJ_sc_sJ_s^{\mathsf T}ds.$$ Indeed the right side is continuous finite variation and the product minus it is a martingale, so uniqueness follows from [F2]. Uniqueness also follows in the energy completion, and the construction extends to every predictable $J$ of finite $c$ energy by truncation: $J1_{\{\|J\|\le k\}}$ lies in $L^2(\mu)$ and converges in energy by dominated convergence.

Since $H$ is bounded and predictable, step 2.1 applies. Set $B^{(n)}=I_{M^{\tau_n}}(H)$. The constructions agree up to the smaller localizer. For elementary integrands the stopping identity is the defining increment identity, with the stopped integrator; extension follows by the maximal bound, since the energy restricted to a stopped interval is no greater than the full energy. This comparison also applies when the two approximation sequences differ, by uniqueness of the energy completion. Therefore the $B^{(n)}$ paste to an adapted continuous local martingale $B=\int H\,dM$, with $$[B]_t=\int_0^tH_sa_sH_s^{\mathsf T}ds=tI_d.$$ This first constructs $B$ in the augmented filtration; [A1] makes it Brownian there. It has an adapted version in the original filtration: choose an increasing subsequence of localizers, still denoted by $\tau_n$, with $P(\tau_n<T)\le2^{-n}$, and original elementary $G_n$ approximating $H$ in the corresponding stopped energy so well that $P(\sup_{t\le T}|I_{M^{\tau_n}}(G_n)_t-B^{\tau_n}_t|>2^{-n})\le2^{-n}$. Steps 1.2–2.1 provide these choices. The unstopped elementary sums $I_M(G_n)$ are adapted to the original filtration; on $\{\tau_n=T\}$ they equal the stopped sums. The union bound and summability therefore give uniform almost-sure convergence to $B$ on a common full event. Define the value at each time as their pointwise limit when finite and zero otherwise. This gives the desired original-adapted version, with the same continuous paths and bracket almost surely. Its Brownian increments in the augmented filtration are independent of every earlier event in the original subfiltration as well. Thus the original-adapted version is Brownian in the original filtration. The Lévy supplier's proof uses only the stated finite set of times in $[0,T]$, so it needs no extension past $T$.

We prove the recovery identity rather than assume an associativity rule. Fix $n$ and write $N=M^{\tau_n}$ and $Z=B^{\tau_n}=I_N(H)$. For bounded elementary $K$, its defining sum against $Z$ is $I_N(KH)$. On one block, this follows by approximating $H$ in step 2.1: multiplication by the bounded left-measurable block coefficient and restriction to that block commute with both elementary sums and their $L^2$ limits; sum over the finitely many blocks. The right integral exists because $KH$ is bounded predictable. For the stopped Brownian motion $Z$, the coordinate product-compensators are also true martingales. Brownian Doob bounds give $E\sup_{t\le T}|B_t|^2<\infty$, so stopping the Brownian coordinate and product martingales is justified by the same finite-valued approximation and $L^1$ domination. Therefore the elementary isometry and maximal bound of step 1.3 apply to $Z$ as well. Since $[Z]_t=(t\wedge\tau_n)I_d$, elementary integrals against $Z$ have energy $E\int_0^{T\wedge\tau_n}\|K_s\|_F^2ds$. Applying steps 1.2–2.1 with this finite measure defines their completion, namely the stopped predictable Brownian integral. Choose elementary $K_j$ converging to $\sigma$ for that energy; this is possible since $E\int_0^{T\wedge\tau_n}\|\sigma_s\|_F^2ds\le n$. For the right integrals the exact identity $$E\int_0^{T\wedge\tau_n}\operatorname{tr}\bigl((K_j-\sigma)H a H^{\mathsf T}(K_j-\sigma)^{\mathsf T}\bigr)ds=E\int_0^{T\wedge\tau_n}\|K_j-\sigma\|_F^2ds$$ shows convergence to $I_N(\sigma H)=I_N(I_d)=N$. The left sums converge to $\int\sigma\,dZ$ in the same maximal norm. Thus $\int_0^{t\wedge\tau_n}\sigma_s\,dB_s=M_{t\wedge\tau_n}$. Letting $n$ increase proves the recovery identity on all of $[0,T]$, with the usual predictable Brownian integral defined by these localized elementary completions.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and let $u:U\to\mathbb R$ be locally semiconvex: around each point there is a Euclidean ball ([[def-metric-ball]]) and $c\ge0$ such that $x\mapsto u(x)+c|x|^2/2$ is convex in the sense of [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]. Outside a set null in the cube-cover sense of [[def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn]], there are $p\in\mathbb R^n$ and a symmetric matrix $A$ with
$$u(x+h)=u(x)+p\cdot h+\tfrac12h^{\mathsf T}Ah+o(|h|^2)\quad(h\to0).$$
The remainder is uniform in direction. In particular $u$ is twice differentiable in the Peano sense almost everywhere.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be any measure space, let $1 < p < \infty$, and let
$q$ be conjugate to $p$. For every bounded linear functional
$\Lambda:L^p(\mu)\to\mathbb R$ there exists a unique $g \in L^q(\mu)$ such that
$$\Lambda([f])=\int fg\,d\mu\qquad([f]\in L^p(\mu)).$$
Moreover,
$$\|\Lambda\|=\|g\|_q.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then
$$\lim_{r\to0^+}A_rf(x)=f(x)$$
for Lebesgue-almost every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Assume Countable Choice for Lebesgue integration. Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. Fix $\rho\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$ with $\int\rho=1$, and put $\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$ for $\varepsilon>0$. The smooth local convolution $f_\varepsilon(x)=u(\rho_\varepsilon(x-\cdot))$ is defined on $V_\varepsilon=\{x:x-\varepsilon\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\Omega\}$. Its regular distribution converges weakly to $u$ locally: every test $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ is supported in $V_\varepsilon$ for all sufficiently small positive $\varepsilon$, and $\int f_\varepsilon\psi\to u(\psi)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $\bigl(x^{(j)}\bigr)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$
be a sequence in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whose range
$\{\, x^{(j)} : j \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ is a bounded subset of
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).
Then there are a strictly increasing $i : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
([[def-sequence]], [[lem-index-map-grows]]) and a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$
with

$$x^{(i_j)} \longrightarrow p \quad \text{in } (\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$$

([[def-metric-convergence]]). By [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] the same
statement holds with $d_2$ replaced by the metric of any norm on
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$, boundedness and convergence both being unchanged by that
replacement ([[def-equivalent-norms]]).

**This is assembled from published theorems and is not proved again by
bisection.** The bisection is in [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], published at order 120;
what is added here is the passage from compactness to sequential compactness and
the reading of the conclusion in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

**Choice cost: none.** [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] is proved by bisection and uses no
choice principle, and "compact implies sequentially compact" is a theorem of ZF
([[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]]). The five-way equivalence
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] is **not** used, precisely because it is
stated under countable choice and dependent choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]) and
would overcharge this corollary; the arrow-by-arrow account is
[[rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1} \in \mathbb{R}$
with $a_k \ge 0$ for every $k < n$. Write

$$A := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k<n} a_k, \qquad G := \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)^{1/n},$$

the **arithmetic mean** and the **geometric mean**, where the $n$-th root exists
because $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]],
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]]) and $n$ denotes the canonical field image
$n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural number n, which is invertible since $n \ge 1$
([[lem-of-naturals-positive]], [[lem-of-q-embeds]]). Then

$$\prod_{k<n} a_k \le A^{n}, \qquad \text{equivalently} \qquad G \le A,$$

and equality holds in either form if and only if $a_0 = a_1 = \dots = a_{n-1}$.

The proof is **Cauchy's forward-backward induction**: the statement is proved
first along a doubling sequence, by doubling, and then pulled back from a member
of that sequence to every smaller $n$ by a descent that replaces the missing
entry with the arithmetic mean of the others. That is why the induction below
runs over the doubling scheme and not over $n$ directly.

One point of hygiene decides how the doubling scheme is written. The doubling
index has to be a **natural number**, because it is used as the length of a list,
as a bound on an index, and as the starting point of a descent. The symbol $2^{j}$
would not do: [[def-integer-power]] defines powers of a *real* base, so $2^{j}$
denotes a power of the real field element $2\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ under that definition, rather than a natural-number-valued operation, and so cannot
index anything. The doubling sequence is therefore defined inside $\mathbb{N}$,
by recursion ([[thm-recursion]]):

$$N_0 = 1, \qquad N_{j+1} = N_j + N_j \quad (j \in \mathbb{N}),$$

and the induction below runs over $j$, with $N_j$ as the list length. No
identity relating $N_j$ to any real power is needed anywhere, and none is claimed.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let
$u,v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ be the multi-index of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. We say that $v$ is
the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Both integrals are finite because the test and all its derivatives are bounded
and compactly supported. The test identity is choice-free. By
[[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]] and the signed
transpose convention in [[def-distributional-derivative]], it is equivalent
to $\partial^\alpha T_u=T_v$ as distributions. For $\alpha=0$, this identity
reduces to $T_u=T_v$, hence to $u=v$ almost everywhere by the published
embedding theorem under [[def-countable-choice]].

**Well-definedness.** Changing either representative on a null set leaves each
test integral unchanged. Weak derivatives are therefore statements about
almost-everywhere classes; existence and uniqueness of their locally
integrable value classes are audited separately.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$,
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, and $u,v,w\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$. If both
$v$ and $w$ are weak $\alpha$-derivatives of $u$, then
$$v=w\quad\text{almost everywhere on }\Omega.$$
Thus a weak derivative, when it exists, is unique as an almost-everywhere
class. No connectedness assumption is needed.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the assertion holds because there is only the zero
class and no nonzero tests.

derivations.claim: For each $a\in\mathcal C$, choose unit eigenvectors $e_i(a)$ and eigenvalues $s_i(a)\ge0$, so $a=\sum_{i=1}^d s_i(a)e_i(a)e_i(a)^{\mathsf T}$. For $0<h<1$, define $$L_h^au(t,x)=\sum_i\frac{s_i(a)}{h^2}\bigl(u(t,x+he_i)-2u(t,x)+u(t,x-he_i)\bigr)+\frac{r(a)}h\bigl(u(t+h,x)-u(t,x)\bigr).$$ All off-center coefficients are nonnegative. Their sum is $q_h(a)=2\operatorname{tr}(a)/h^2+r(a)/h$.

Write $L_h^au=M_h^au-q_h(a)u$, where $M_h^a$ is its off-center positive operator, and define $$P_hu(z)=\sup_{a\in\mathcal C}\frac{M_h^au(z)+k(a)f(z)}{\lambda+q_h(a)}.$$ Put $Q_h=2h^{-2}+h^{-1}$ and $\gamma_h=Q_h/(\lambda+Q_h)<1$. Positivity and $M_h^a1=q_h(a)\le Q_h$ give $$\|P_hu-P_hw\|_\infty\le\gamma_h\|u-w\|_\infty.$$ The same argument bounds $\sup(P_hu-P_hw)^+$ by $\gamma_h\sup(u-w)^+$.

Starting with $u_0=0$, iterate $u_{j+1}=P_hu_j$. The contraction bounds successive differences by a summable geometric sequence. Their sums converge uniformly to a bounded function $v_h$, since a uniformly Cauchy sequence of bounded real functions has a bounded pointwise limit and converges uniformly. The contraction estimate gives $P_hv_h=v_h$ and uniqueness among bounded fixed points. Multiplying the individual residuals by their denominators, which lie in $[\lambda,\lambda+Q_h]$, shows that this is equivalent to $$\sup_{a\in\mathcal C}\{L_h^av_h-\lambda v_h+k(a)f\}=0.\qquad\text{(1)}$$.

AM–GM applied to $r(a),s_1(a),\ldots,s_d(a)$, whose sum is $1$, gives $0\le k(a)\le1/n$. Hence $P_h$ preserves $0\le u\le V$: at the upper bound its numerator is at most $q_h(a)V+\|f\|_\infty/n=(\lambda+q_h(a))V$. Thus $0\le v_h\le V$.

If $u$ has Lipschitz constant at most $L$, each affine control expression in $P_hu$ has Lipschitz constant at most $$\frac{q_h(a)L+L_f/n}{\lambda+q_h(a)}\le L.$$ A supremum preserves this common bound. Iteration and uniform convergence therefore make every $v_h$ globally $L$-Lipschitz.

If $u(z)+N|z|^2$ is convex, every translate of $u$ has the same semiconvexity constant $N$. The numerator in each affine control expression has semiconvexity constant at most $q_h(a)N+N_f/n$. After division this is at most $N$, since $N_f/n=\lambda N$. Adding $N|z|^2$ makes each expression convex; the translation corrections to its quadratic term are affine plus constants. Their supremum is convex. Starting from $0$ and passing to the uniform limit proves that $v_h+N|z|^2$ is convex.

Take a sequence $h_j\downarrow0$. Diagonally select a subsequence along which $v_{h_j}$ converges at every rational point. Boundedness gives the successive subsequences, and finite rational nets plus the common Lipschitz constant give uniform convergence on every compact set. Call the limit $v$. It satisfies $0\le v\le V$, the global $L$-Lipschitz bound, and convexity of $v+N|z|^2$.

Let $\psi$ be a supersolution as in the Statement. The centered second difference is an average of the corresponding directional second derivative, and the forward time difference is an average of $\partial_t\psi$. Bounded uniform continuity gives $E_h\to0$ such that, uniformly in $z$ and $a$, $$\left|L_h^a\psi-r(a)\partial_t\psi-a:D_x^2\psi\right|\le E_h.$$ For example, the sum of the spatial-Hessian and time-derivative moduli of continuity at scale $h$ suffices, since $r(a)+\operatorname{tr}a=1$. Therefore $\Psi_h=\psi+E_h/\lambda$ satisfies $P_h\Psi_h\le\Psi_h$.

The one-sided contraction estimate gives $$\sup(v_h-\Psi_h)^+\le\gamma_h\sup(v_h-\Psi_h)^+.$$ The supremum is finite, so it vanishes. Pass along the chosen subsequence to obtain $v\le\psi$. This proves the comparison assertion for the same constructed limit.

Fix $a\in\mathcal C$ and a nonnegative compactly supported smooth test $\eta$. Equation (1) implies $L_h^av_h-\lambda v_h+k(a)f\le0$. Integrate against $\eta$ and transfer translations to $\eta$. Its adjoint centered differences converge uniformly, on a common compact support, to the spatial second derivatives; its adjoint forward difference converges to $-\partial_t\eta$. Local uniform convergence of $v_h$ gives $$\int v\bigl(a:D_x^2\eta-r(a)\partial_t\eta-\lambda\eta\bigr)+\int k(a)f\eta\le0.\qquad\text{(2)}$$ Thus each fixed-control inequality holds as a distribution.

We will use this elementary representation fact on a bounded open ball $B$: if a linear functional $T$ on compact smooth tests satisfies $|T\eta|\le C\|\eta\|_1$, it is integration against a function of absolute value at most $C$. Indeed, $\|\eta\|_1\le |B|^{1/2}\|\eta\|_2$ extends $T$ continuously from the dense test subspace to $L^2(B)$. Real $L^2$ duality represents it by $g\in L^2(B)$. The original $L^1$ estimate extends to all $L^2$ tests, because their $L^2$ approximations also converge in $L^1$. Test with $\operatorname{sgn}(g)\mathbf1_{\{|g|>C+\epsilon\}}$ to obtain a contradiction unless that set is null. Hence $|g|\le C$. The unique local representatives agree on overlaps.

Choose a nonnegative smooth compactly supported unit-mass kernel $\rho$ and put $\rho_\epsilon(z)=\epsilon^{-n}\rho(z/\epsilon)$, $v_\epsilon=v*\rho_\epsilon$. The common Lipschitz bound gives $|D_zv_\epsilon|\le L$, and $v_\epsilon\to v$ locally uniformly. Integration by parts bounds each distributional directional derivative by $L\|\eta\|_1$. Step 1.2 represents these by bounded weak derivatives. Using a countable dense set of unit directions gives $|D_zv|\le L$ almost everywhere.

Semiconvexity gives $D_z^2v_\epsilon\ge-2NI$. For a unit spatial vector $e$, insert the rank-one control $a=ee^{\mathsf T}$ into (2). It has $r(a)=k(a)=0$, so $D_{ee}v-\lambda v\le0$ as distributions. Convolution makes this $D_{ee}v_\epsilon\le\lambda v_\epsilon$ everywhere. Taking a countable dense set of $e$ and then continuity yields $$-2NI\le D_x^2v_\epsilon\le\lambda v_\epsilon I\le\lambda VI.\qquad\text{(3)}$$.

Set $C=\max(2N,\lambda V)$. Every spatial Hessian entry in (3) has absolute value at most $C$. For a compact smooth test $\eta$, $$\int v\,\partial_{x_ix_j}\eta=\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\int (D_{ij}v_\epsilon)\eta.$$ Step 1.2 therefore represents this distribution by an actual weak derivative $D_{ij}v\in L^\infty$, with norm at most $C$. Passing the directional bounds through tests gives $-2NI\le D_x^2v\le\lambda vI$ almost everywhere. The control $a=0$ in (2) similarly gives $\partial_tv\le\lambda v$.

Each individually existing derivative commutes with convolution by its weak-test identity: if $g=D^\beta v$, where $\beta$ is a first index or two spatial indices, test against $y\mapsto\rho_\epsilon(z-y)$ to obtain $$D^\beta(v*\rho_\epsilon)(z)=\int g(y)\rho_\epsilon(z-y)\,dy.$$ The factors $(-1)^{|\beta|}$ cancel. This argument uses only that particular weak derivative. All expressions in (2) now have bounded-function representatives. Discard the null sets for a countable dense subset of $\mathcal C$; continuity in $a$, including continuity of the determinant at singular matrices, extends the inequalities to every $a$ on one common full-measure set.

By semiconvexity and the local Alexandrov theorem, almost every $z_0$ has a direction-uniform expansion $v(z)=q(z)+o(|z-z_0|^2)$ for a quadratic polynomial $q$ with $q(z_0)=v(z_0)$. Require also that ball averages recover each bounded weak first and spatial second derivative $g$, and $g^2$, at $z_0$. These finitely many requirements remove only a null set. Expanding the square gives $$\frac{1}{|B(z_0,s)|}\int_{B(z_0,s)}|g-g(z_0)|^2\longrightarrow0,$$ so Cauchy–Schwarz gives mean absolute convergence as well.

The first-order blowups $[v(z_0+sy)-v(z_0)]/s$ converge locally uniformly to $Dq(z_0)\cdot y$. Their weak derivatives are $D_zv(z_0+sy)$, which converge locally in $L^1$ to the weak derivative values at $z_0$ by step 10.2. Distributional limits identify those values with $Dq(z_0)$. Similarly the second-order blowups $$\frac{v(z_0+sy)-v(z_0)-sDq(z_0)\cdot y}{s^2}$$ converge locally uniformly to $\tfrac12y^{\mathsf T}D^2q\,y$, while their spatial second weak derivatives are $D_x^2v(z_0+sy)$ and converge locally in $L^1$ to $D_x^2v(z_0)$. Thus the spatial block of $D^2q$ equals that actual weak Hessian. These scaled weak identities follow directly by changing variables in the compact-test identities.

Fix $\epsilon>0$ and set $q_\pm(z)=q(z)\pm\epsilon|z-z_0|^2$. On a sufficiently small closed ball centered at $z_0$, the expansion makes $q_+$ a strict upper contact and $q_-$ a strict lower contact. Let $z_j$ maximize $v_{h_j}-q_+$ there. Local uniform convergence implies $z_j\to z_0$ and $m_j=(v_{h_j}-q_+)(z_j)\to0$. For large $j$, every stencil neighbor of $z_j$ remains in that ball. Nonnegative off-center weights then give $$0\le\sup_a\{L_{h_j}^aq_+-\lambda q_++k(a)f\}(z_j)-\lambda m_j$$.

Centered spatial differences are exact on a quadratic polynomial; its forward time difference differs from its time derivative by $h_j\partial_{tt}q_+/2$. This error is uniform in the controls, since $0\le r(a)\le1$. Bounded coefficients and uniform Lipschitz continuity of $f$ therefore allow passage in step 11.2 to $$\max_a\{r(a)\partial_tq_++a:D_x^2q_+-\lambda q_++k(a)f\}(z_0)\ge0$$.

Minimize $v_{h_j}-q_-$ on the same ball. The identical positive-weight calculation reverses the inequality and gives the corresponding maximum for $q_-$ nonpositive in the limit. Let $\epsilon\downarrow0$ in both conclusions. Continuity of the finite-dimensional maximum gives zero for $q$. By step 11.1 its first and spatial second coefficients are the actual weak derivatives of $v$ at $z_0$. This proves the asserted Bellman equation outside a null set.

At a point where the equation and derivative bounds hold, put $S=\lambda v-\partial_tv\ge0$ and $H=\lambda vI-D_x^2v\ge0$. The equation becomes $$\max_{\substack{r\ge0,\ a\ge0\\r+\operatorname{tr}a=1}}\{-rS-a:H+(r\det a)^{1/n}f\}=0.\qquad\text{(4)}$$ In particular every normalized control satisfies $rS+a:H\ge(r\det a)^{1/n}f$.

For $\delta>0$, let $S_\delta=S+\delta$, $H_\delta=H+\delta I$, and $$c_\delta=(S_\delta^{-1}+\operatorname{tr}H_\delta^{-1})^{-1},\qquad r_\delta=c_\delta/S_\delta,\qquad a_\delta=c_\delta H_\delta^{-1}.$$ This is a normalized control, and $$r_\delta S+a_\delta:H\le nc_\delta,\qquad (r_\delta\det a_\delta)^{1/n}=\frac{c_\delta}{(S_\delta\det H_\delta)^{1/n}}.$$ Insert it into the inequality from step 14.1 and cancel $c_\delta>0$ to get $f\le n(S_\delta\det H_\delta)^{1/n}$. Sending $\delta\downarrow0$ gives $f\le n(S\det H)^{1/n}$, including $S=0$ or singular $H$.

If $S>0$ and $H$ is positive definite, AM–GM for $rS$ and the eigenvalues of $a^{1/2}Ha^{1/2}$ gives $$rS+a:H\ge n(r\det a\,S\det H)^{1/n}.$$ If $f<n(S\det H)^{1/n}$, the expression in (4) is strictly negative for interior controls. It is also strictly negative for boundary controls: there $r\det a=0$, whereas $rS+a:H>0$ because $r+\operatorname{tr}a=1$. Compactness of the normalized control set and continuity make its maximum strictly negative, contradicting (4). Thus equality holds. If $S=0$ or $H$ is singular, step 15.1 already gives $f=0$ and $S\det H=0$. This proves the product identity in all cases, and completes every assertion.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $\lambda>0$, and let $f:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded. Suppose that $f$ is globally Lipschitz with constant $L_f$ and that $f(z)+N_f|z|^2$ is convex for some $N_f\ge0$, where $z=(t,x)$. Set
$$n=d+1,\qquad V=\frac{\|f\|_\infty}{n\lambda},\qquad L=\frac{L_f}{n\lambda},\qquad N=\frac{N_f}{n\lambda}.$$
Define
$$\mathcal C=\{a\in\operatorname{Sym}_d:a\ge0,\ \operatorname{tr}a\le1\},\qquad r(a)=1-\operatorname{tr}a,\qquad k(a)=(r(a)\det a)^{1/n}.$$
There is a globally $L$-Lipschitz function $v:\mathbb R^{d+1}\to[0,V]$ such that $v(z)+N|z|^2$ is convex. Its weak derivatives $\partial_tv$, $D_iv$ and $D_{ij}v$, $1\le i,j\le d$, exist and are bounded. They satisfy
$$|D_zv|\le L,\qquad -2NI\le D_x^2v\le\lambda vI\quad\text{almost everywhere},$$
and, outside one common null set,
$$\max_{a\in\mathcal C}\{r(a)\partial_tv+a:D_x^2v-\lambda v+k(a)f\}=0.$$
In particular, with $S=\lambda v-\partial_tv$ and $H=\lambda vI-D_x^2v$,
$$S\ge0,\qquad H\ge0,\qquad S\det H=\left(\frac{f}{d+1}\right)^{d+1}\quad\text{almost everywhere}.$$
For each fixed $a\in\mathcal C$, the corresponding linear expression is also nonpositive as a distribution.

The same $v$ can be chosen below every bounded smooth function $\psi$ for which $\partial_t\psi,D_x^2\psi$ are bounded and uniformly continuous and
$$\sup_{a\in\mathcal C}\{r(a)\partial_t\psi+a:D_x^2\psi-\lambda\psi+k(a)f\}\le0\quad\text{everywhere}.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1} \in \mathbb{R}$
with $a_k \ge 0$ for every $k < n$. Write

$$A := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k<n} a_k, \qquad G := \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)^{1/n},$$

the **arithmetic mean** and the **geometric mean**, where the $n$-th root exists
because $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]],
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]]) and $n$ denotes the canonical field image
$n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural number n, which is invertible since $n \ge 1$
([[lem-of-naturals-positive]], [[lem-of-q-embeds]]). Then

$$\prod_{k<n} a_k \le A^{n}, \qquad \text{equivalently} \qquad G \le A,$$

and equality holds in either form if and only if $a_0 = a_1 = \dots = a_{n-1}$.

The proof is **Cauchy's forward-backward induction**: the statement is proved
first along a doubling sequence, by doubling, and then pulled back from a member
of that sequence to every smaller $n$ by a descent that replaces the missing
entry with the arithmetic mean of the others. That is why the induction below
runs over the doubling scheme and not over $n$ directly.

One point of hygiene decides how the doubling scheme is written. The doubling
index has to be a **natural number**, because it is used as the length of a list,
as a bound on an index, and as the starting point of a descent. The symbol $2^{j}$
would not do: [[def-integer-power]] defines powers of a *real* base, so $2^{j}$
denotes a power of the real field element $2\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ under that definition, rather than a natural-number-valued operation, and so cannot
index anything. The doubling sequence is therefore defined inside $\mathbb{N}$,
by recursion ([[thm-recursion]]):

$$N_0 = 1, \qquad N_{j+1} = N_j + N_j \quad (j \in \mathbb{N}),$$

and the induction below runs over $j$, with $N_j$ as the list length. No
identity relating $N_j$ to any real power is needed anywhere, and none is claimed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then
$$\lim_{r\to0^+}A_rf(x)=f(x)$$
for Lebesgue-almost every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: Take $v$ from [F1]. Put $\rho(x)=\sqrt{1+|x|^2}$, $\eta=1/4$, and $U(x)=C\exp(-\eta\rho(x))$. Then $D_x^2U=U(\eta^2D\rho\otimes D\rho-\eta D^2\rho)\le\eta^2UI$. For normalized $A,r$ the Bellman expression of $U$ is at most $-[r+(1-\eta^2)\operatorname{tr}A]U+f/(d+1)\le-(1-\eta^2)U+f/(d+1)$ by [F2]. Choose finite $C$ to make this nonpositive on the compact spatial support of $f$; it is nonpositive elsewhere as well. This bounded smooth $U$ has the bounded uniformly continuous derivatives required for comparison. Hence $v(t,x)\le C\exp(-\eta\rho(x))$ uniformly in $t$.

Write $F(t)=\sup_xf(t,x)$, supported in $[a,b]$. Choose smooth compactly supported $g\ge F$ so that $U(t)=\int_t^\infty e^{t-s}g(s)ds\ge F(t)$ everywhere: after choosing a smooth compact majorant of $F$, add a sufficiently large positive smooth bump in $(b+1,b+2)$, whose convolution has positive minimum on $[a,b]$. Since $U_t=U-g$, its normalized Bellman expression is $-rg-(1-r)U+(r\det A)^{1/(d+1)}f\le-F+f/(d+1)\le0$. Comparison applies, so $0\le v\le U$ and $v=0$ after the right endpoint of $\operatorname{supp}g$.

For symmetric $B$ let $c_m(B)=(-1)^me_m(B)$, the signed sum of order-$m$ principal minors, with $c_0=1$, and define the matrix differential $C_m$ by $dc_m(B)[E]=C_m(B):E$. Polynomial expansion and homogeneity give $$\det(zI-B)=\sum_{m=0}^dz^{d-m}c_m(B),\qquad C_m(B):B=mc_m(B).$$ For $B\le0$, $C_m(B)\le0$ when $m\ge1$: differentiating each principal minor of $-B$ gives minus an embedded positive semidefinite cofactor matrix, including singular cases by continuity. For smooth $w$, each row and column of $C_m(D^2w)$ has zero divergence. Indeed expand its minors as signed sums over permutations; every differentiated Hessian factor gives a third derivative, canceled by the term with the differentiated row transposed with that factor's row. The signs reverse and the mixed third derivatives coincide; order-one minors have constant differentials. This proves the divergence identity by finite polynomial calculation.

Comparing coefficients in $\det(zI-B)=\det((z-h)I-(B-hI))$ and differentiating in $B$ at fixed $h\ge0$ gives $$C_m(B)=\sum_{k=1}^m(-1)^{m-k}\binom{d-k}{m-k}h^{m-k}C_k(B-hI).$$ Thus $\sum_{m=1}^dw_mh^{d-m}C_m(B)=\sum_{k=1}^d\beta_kh^{d-k}C_k(B-hI)$, where $\beta_k=\sum_{j=0}^{d-k}(-1)^j\binom{d-k}{j}w_{k+j}$. If $hI-B\ge0$ and every $\beta_k\ge0$, this matrix is negative semidefinite by step 1.2. Set $p=d+2$. The two sequences needed below are $a_m=(p-m-1)/(m+1)$ and $b_m=1/[m(m+1)]$. For $n=d-k\ge1$, the alternating difference of $a$ is $p\int_0^1t^k(1-t)^ndt\ge0$; for $n=0$ it is $a_d>0$. That of $b$ is $\int_0^1t^{k-1}(1-t)^{n+1}dt\ge0$. These integral formulas follow by expanding $(1-t)^n$. Both matrix sums are therefore negative semidefinite whenever $hI-B\ge0$.

First let $u\ge0$ be smooth, $uI-D_x^2u\ge0$, $u-u_t\ge0$, zero for $t\ge T_1$, with itself and every derivative used below exponentially decaying in $x$ on finite time intervals. Fix $t$ and put $w(s,x)=e^{-s}u(s,x)$, so $w_s\le0$ and $wI-D_x^2w\ge0$. For $m=0,\ldots,d$ set $$A_m=-\int_t^{T_1}\!\int_{\mathbb R^d}w^{p-m-1}c_m(D_x^2w)w_s\,dxds.$$ Then $A=\sum_mA_m=\int_t^{T_1}\int w^{p-d-1}(-w_s)\det(wI-D_x^2w)$. Temporal integration by parts gives the initial term $(p-m)^{-1}\int w(t)^{p-m}c_m(D_x^2w(t))$ plus $(p-m)^{-1}\int_t^{T_1}\int w^{p-m}C_m(D_x^2w):D_x^2w_s$. Two spatial integrations by parts, the divergence identity and Euler identity in step 1.2 yield $$(m+1)A_m=\frac{\int w(t)^{p-m}c_m(D_x^2w(t))dx}{p-m}+(p-m-1)\int_t^{T_1}\!\int w^{p-m-2}w_s(D_xw)^{\mathsf T}C_m(D_x^2w)D_xw\,dxds.$$ These integrations can first use compact spatial cutoffs. Every boundary error vanishes by exponential decay, and all integrals are absolutely convergent on the finite time interval, justifying Fubini. No power is singular since $p=d+2$.

Sum the identity in step 2.3. Its final integrals are nonnegative: their matrix is $w^{p-d-2}\sum_ma_mw^{d-m}C_m(D_x^2w)\le0$ by step 2.2, and $w_s\le0$. Therefore $A\ge\sum_m[(p-m)(m+1)]^{-1}\int w(t)^{p-m}c_m(D_x^2w(t))dx$. For $m\ge1$, substitute $c_m=m^{-1}C_m:D_x^2w$ and integrate once in space. Their sum becomes $$-\int w(t)^{p-d-1}(D_xw)^{\mathsf T}\Bigl[\sum_{m=1}^db_mw(t)^{d-m}C_m(D_x^2w)\Bigr]D_xw\,dx\ge0$$ by step 2.2. The $m=0$ term is $p^{-1}\int w(t)^pdx$. Consequently $$p e^{pt}\int_t^{T_1}e^{-ps}\!\int u^{p-d-1}(u-u_s)\det(uI-D_x^2u)dxds\ge\int u(t,x)^pdx$$.

Restrict the nonnegative $u$ to any spatial line. The scalar inequality $y''\le y$ gives $y(r)\le y(0)\cosh r+y'(0)\sinh r$ by variation of constants for $y''-y$. Nonnegativity for all $r\ge0$ implies $y'(0)\ge-y(0)$; reversing the direction gives $|D_xu|\le u$. Integrating the derivative inequality along a segment gives $u(t,x)\ge u(t,y)e^{-|x-y|}$ (or first use $u+\delta$ and let $\delta\downarrow0$). Therefore $$\int u(t,x)^pdx\ge c_du(t,y)^p,\qquad c_d=\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-p|x|}dx>0.$$ This constant is finite and depends only on $d$, since $p=d+2$.

Convolve the weak solution $v$ from step 1.1 in spacetime with a nonnegative smooth unit-mass kernel of radius $\epsilon$, and write $v_\epsilon$. It is nonnegative, has $v_\epsilon-(v_\epsilon)_t\ge0$ and $v_\epsilon I-D_x^2v_\epsilon\ge0$ by the linear weak inequalities and [F3]. For each fixed $\epsilon$, all derivatives decay exponentially in $x$ by step 1.1 and kernel differentiation; step 2.1 supplies a finite future cutoff. Hence steps 3.1–3.2 apply to $v_\epsilon$. At almost every spacetime point [F3] and [F1] give $$(v_\epsilon-(v_\epsilon)_t)\det(v_\epsilon I-D_x^2v_\epsilon)\longrightarrow(f/(d+1))^{d+1}.$$ All the weak derivatives occurring here are bounded uniformly after convolution. On any fixed finite time interval $[a,T_1+1]$, the integrand in step 3.1 is dominated by a constant times $e^{-\eta|x|}$: the factor $v_\epsilon^{p-d-1}$ is precisely $v_\epsilon$, with uniform exponential decay, and the remaining determinant factors are uniformly bounded. Thus [F4] gives the exact needed dominated limit. Also $v_\epsilon(t,y)\to v(t,y)$ at every point by Lipschitz continuity. We obtain $$c_dv(t,y)^p\le\frac{p}{(d+1)^{d+1}}\int_t^\infty e^{-p(s-t)}\!\int v(s,x)^{p-d-1}f(s,x)^{d+1}dxds$$.

Fix finite $a$ and put $V_a=\sup_{s\ge a,x}v(s,x)<\infty$. For $t\ge a$, step 4.1 is bounded above by $p(d+1)^{-d-1}V_a^{p-d-1}\|f\|_{d+1}^{d+1}$. Taking the supremum in $(t,y)$ gives $c_dV_a^p\le p(d+1)^{-d-1}V_a^{p-d-1}\|f\|_{d+1}^{d+1}$. If $V_a=0$ there is nothing to prove; otherwise divide to obtain $V_a\le[p/(c_d(d+1)^{d+1})]^{1/(d+1)}\|f\|_{d+1}$. This constant is independent of $a$, so it bounds $v$ everywhere. Applying the line argument in step 3.2 to the spatially smoothed weak solution and passing to Lebesgue points gives $|D_xv|\le v$ almost everywhere. Finally rescale the normalized control inequalities of [F1] using $r=1/(1+\operatorname{tr}A)$ and normalized matrix $rA$; divide by $r>0$ to get the asserted inequality for every $A\ge0$. The common null set is obtained first for countably many dense matrices and then by continuity. Steps 1.1 and 2.1 supply the additional decay and future cutoff.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. For each dimension $d\ge1$ there is a finite constant $C_d$ such that for every nonnegative $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d)$ there exists a bounded nonnegative globally Lipschitz function $v$, with bounded weak derivatives $v_t,D_xv,D_x^2v$, satisfying
$$\|v\|_\infty\le C_d\|f\|_{L^{d+1}(\mathbb R^{d+1})},\qquad |D_xv|\le v\quad\hbox{almost everywhere},$$
and, simultaneously for every constant symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $A$,
$$v_t+A:D_x^2v-(1+\operatorname{tr}A)v+(\det A)^{1/(d+1)}f\le0$$
as distributions and as bounded-function inequalities almost everywhere. One can choose $v$ to decay exponentially in $|x|$ uniformly in time and to vanish for all sufficiently large future times. The derivative bounds used in constructing $v$ may depend on derivatives of $f$; the displayed height constant does not.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]: $B$ is a standard Brownian
motion on a filtered probability space, adapted to $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$,
with $B_t-B_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ of law $N(0,t-s)$ for $0\le s<t$.
For this localized-calculus definition the filtration satisfies the usual
conditions, as required by
[[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]].

1. **Real continuous Brownian Ito process.** A real progressively measurable process
   $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **continuous Brownian Ito process** when there are
   * a finite real $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $X_0$,
   * a real progressively measurable process $b=(b_s)_{s\ge0}$
     [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]] with
     $\int_0^t|b_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every finite $t\ge0$, and
   * a real predictable process $\sigma=(\sigma_s)_{s\ge0}$, locally
     square-integrable in the sense that $\int_0^t\sigma_s^2\,ds<\infty$
     almost surely for every finite $t$
     [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]],

   such that, up to equality at all times on a measurable probability-one event,
   $$X_t=X_0+\int_0^tb_s\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s,\qquad t\ge0,$$
   where the first integral is the pathwise Lebesgue integral of $s\mapsto
   b_s(\omega)$ and the second is the localized Ito integral
   $\sigma\cdot B$ of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. One writes
   $\displaystyle dX_t=b_t\,dt+\sigma_t\,dB_t$ for the display, and $b$ is
   called the **drift** and $\sigma$ the **diffusion coefficient** of this
   representation.

2. **Multidimensional Brownian-driven process.** Let $d\ge1$ and $m\ge1$ be
   finite integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional
   Brownian motion [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] that is adapted to
   $(\mathcal F_t)$ and whose vector increment $B_t-B_s$ is independent of
   $\mathcal F_s$ for $0\le s<t$, let $X_0$ be a finite
   $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vector, let $b$ be an
   $\mathbb R^d$-valued progressively measurable process with
   $\int_0^t|b^i_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every $i$ and finite $t$, and let
   $\sigma=(\sigma^{ik})$ be an $\mathbb R^{d\times m}$-valued predictable
   process, each entry predictable
   [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]], with
   $\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every $i,k$ and finite $t$.
   Then
   $$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
   defines an $\mathbb R^d$-valued **continuous Brownian Ito process** driven by
   $B$, using the progressive integral versions of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. Other progressive representatives agreeing on one measurable full event at every time represent the same process. No claim is made that an arbitrary null-path modification remains adapted.

The following well-definedness clauses are part of the definition and are used
throughout.

3. **The drift integral is a genuine pathwise integral.** Progressive
   measurability gives measurable sections and makes the positive and negative
   integrals $\mathcal F_t$-measurable by the parameter-integral part of Tonelli
   [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], applied to Lebesgue measure on $[0,t]$ and the probability measure on $\mathcal F_t$.
   On the event where both extended integrals are finite, their difference is
   the drift integral; set it to zero otherwise. This is an adapted measurable
   convention, is finite everywhere, and on one probability-one event is
   absolutely continuous on every finite interval (take the countable
   intersection over integer horizons). It is progressive: the map
   $(t,\omega)\mapsto\int_0^tb_s(\omega)\,ds$, with the preceding finite-value
   convention, is measurable on every $[0,T]\times\Omega$ by parameter
   integration, and is adapted. Thus the definition uses the standard
   almost-sure drift and local-energy classes under the usual conditions.

4. **The stochastic integral exists, is unique and is continuous.** By
   [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]] and
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]] the localized integral $\sigma\cdot B$ is a
   well-defined adapted process with continuous paths, unique up to
   indistinguishability, and each of its finite-energy pieces is a
   square-integrable martingale. The displayed integral representative is progressive; $X$ is adapted by its required progressive measurability and has
   continuous paths, $X_t$ is finite almost surely for each $t$, and
   $M^i_t:=\sum_k\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s$ is a continuous local
   martingale relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ in the sense of
   [[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]] for every $i$, with the common energy localizers described in clause 6.

5. **The coefficients are not part of the process.** A continuous Brownian Ito
   process may admit several representations $X=X_0+b\cdot\mathrm{Leb}
   +\sigma\cdot B$ with different pointwise representatives $(b,\sigma)$ (for example, altering a coefficient only at the single time zero), even for the same Brownian
   motion and filtration; this does not assert nonuniqueness of their equivalence classes modulo $\mathrm dt\otimes P$; conversely, two processes with the same displayed
   integral representation and the same $X_0$ are indistinguishable. Every
   statement on this page that mentions a decomposition uses only properties
   common to all representations of the given process. The separate
   quadratic-covariation definition that follows this item on its owning page
   is formulated from $X$ itself and not from $(b,\sigma)$; no
   quadratic-covariation definition is made inside this item.

6. **The class is closed under stopping and under linear combinations.**
   If $\tau$ is a stopping time, the literal stopped process $X^\tau$ is
   progressive. Indeed on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ the map
   $(t,\omega)\mapsto(t\wedge\tau(\omega),\omega)$ is measurable into
   $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal F_T$: the truncated time $\tau\wedge T$
   is $\mathcal F_T$-measurable, minimum is continuous, and rectangle inverse
   images give the assertion. Compose with the progressive restriction of $X$.
   Its drift is $b1_{[0,\tau]}$ and its diffusion is
   $\sigma1_{[0,\tau]}$; these retain almost-sure integrability and the required
   progressive/predictable measurability. The drift identity is pathwise.
   For the stochastic identity, apply the finite-energy stopping identity of
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]], clause 4, on the canonical energy intervals
   of $\sigma$. The truncated integrand has finite energy on these same
   intervals. Comparing its canonical intervals with them at their pairwise
   minima by clause 4 identifies the localized integrals there. Countably
   many full-event agreements and exhaustion then give the identity at all
   times on one full event. Thus stopping closure uses localization, not a
   direct application of clause 4 to a possibly infinite-energy integrand.
   For finitely many coefficients, use the common continuous energy
   $E_t=\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2ds$ and times
   $\kappa_n=\inf\{t:E_t\ge n\}\wedge n$, $n\ge1$.
   The same continuous-energy test as in the local-integrability definition
   makes these stopping times increasing to infinity almost surely, and bounds
   every stopped coefficient's expected energy by $n$. The preceding
   pairwise-minimum comparison shows that every integral stopped there is its
   finite-energy integral. Finite sums of these square-integrable martingales
   are martingales: finite sums preserve adaptation and integrability, and summing the integral test over any $A\in\mathcal F_s$ proves the conditional-expectation identity; hence their sums
   are local martingales with this common sequence. For fixed real constants,
   finite linear combinations of processes driven by the same vector Brownian
   motion have the combined coefficients. Their integrability follows from
   the triangle inequality and $(\sum_{j=1}^r u_j)^2\le r\sum_j u_j^2$.

7. **No pathwise integral against Brownian motion is defined.** The display
   defines the stochastic integral only as the localized limit of
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]; no integral $\int_0^tH_s(\omega)\,dB_s(\omega)$
   along the individual path is asserted, and the page's examples show that
   the pathwise Riemann--Stieltjes route is unavailable.

No choice beyond the declared AC of the ambient interfaces enters the
construction: the coefficients $b,\sigma$ and the process are given data, and
the canonically localized integral is constructed in
[[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. The Axiom of Choice is declared because the
conditional-expectation and $L^2$ interfaces used downstream assume it, and
the countable-choice obligations inherited from those interfaces are declared
as dependencies of this item.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$. For predictable
$H,K$ with finite energy $E\int_0^TH^2ds,E\int_0^TK^2ds<\infty$ the integrals
$\int_0^TH\,dB$ of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] satisfy
$$\int_0^T(H+K)\,dB=\int_0^TH\,dB+\int_0^TK\,dB,\qquad \int_0^T(aH)\,dB=a\int_0^TH\,dB\quad(a\in\mathbb R),$$
and the identities are equalities of $L^2(P)$-classes (almost sure
equalities). Moreover the map $H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is an isometry,
$$E\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)^2=E\int_0^TH^2ds=\|H\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)},$$
it takes values in the mean-zero subspace of $L^2(P)$, and the bilinear cross
identity
$$E\Bigl[\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)\Bigl(\int_0^TK\,dB\Bigr)\Bigr]=E\int_0^TH_sK_s\,ds$$
holds for all such $H,K$. In particular the image of the map is a closed
subspace of $L^2(P)$ isometric to the predictable $L^2$ space of $H$'s, and
$H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is injective up to the $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-class.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). For **every** subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$,
measurable or not,

$$\lambda_n^*(E) \;=\; \inf\,\{\, \lambda_n(U) \;:\; U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \text{ open and } E \subseteq U \,\},$$

the infimum being taken in $[0,+\infty]$ over a family that is nonempty because
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is open.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Fix $f\ge0$ smooth compactly supported, and take $v$ from [F1]. Convolve in spacetime with $\rho_\epsilon(z)=\epsilon^{-d-1}\rho(z/\epsilon)$, where $\rho\ge0$ is a smooth compactly supported unit-mass kernel. Write $v_\epsilon=v*\rho_\epsilon$ and $f_\epsilon=f*\rho_\epsilon$. For each constant $A\ge0$, convolution of the distributional inequality gives $$(v_\epsilon)_t+A:D_x^2v_\epsilon-(1+\operatorname{tr}A)v_\epsilon+(\det A)^{1/(d+1)}f_\epsilon\le0$$ at every spacetime point. These simultaneous inequalities follow first for a countable dense set of matrices and then all matrices by continuity. Also $v_\epsilon\ge0$, $\|v_\epsilon\|_\infty,\|D_xv_\epsilon\|_\infty\le C_d\|f\|_{d+1}$, and $f_\epsilon\to f$ uniformly. Thus evaluation at the random matrix $a_s$ uses smooth pointwise inequalities, with no evaluation of unsmoothed weak derivatives on an unknown occupation measure.

Put $Q_t=\exp(-t-\int_0^{t\wedge\gamma}\operatorname{tr}a_sds)$ and use the Itô formula on $[0,\gamma]$ for $Q_tv_\epsilon(t,Z_t)$. The ordinary product rule with this absolutely continuous scalar factor and step 1.1 give $$d(Qv_\epsilon)\le QD_xv_\epsilon\Sigma\,dW+QD_xv_\epsilon\cdot\beta\,dt-Q(\det a)^{1/(d+1)}f_\epsilon(t,Z_t)dt.$$ The stopped stochastic integral has expected square energy at most $2C_d^2\|f\|_{d+1}^2E\int_0^\gamma\operatorname{tr}a_sds$, hence expectation zero by [F2]. The drift term has integrable absolute value at most $C_d\|f\|_{d+1}E\int_0^\gamma|\beta_s|ds$. The initial and terminal values are bounded nonnegative variables irrespective of $Z_0$. Taking expectations and discarding the terminal value gives the estimate with $f_\epsilon$. The weight obeys $Q_s(\det a_s)^{1/(d+1)}\le C_d(1+\operatorname{tr}a_s)$ by eigenvalue AM–GM, and its stopped integral has finite expectation. Since $\|f_\epsilon\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty$ and $f_\epsilon\to f$ uniformly, [F5] gives dominated convergence for the weighted integrals. Thus $$E\int_0^\gamma Q_s(\det a_s)^{1/(d+1)}f(s,Z_s)ds\le C_d\left(1+E\int_0^\gamma|\beta_s|ds\right)\|f\|_{d+1}.$$ Localization in [F2] can be removed by its square-energy bound and by [F5] for the integrable finite-variation terms.

Define $
u(E)=E\int_0^\gamma Q_s(\det a_s)^{1/(d+1)}1_E(s,Z_s)ds$. It is a finite Borel measure: $Q\le1$ and the eigenvalue AM–GM bound gives $(\det a)^{1/(d+1)}\le C_d(1+\operatorname{tr}a)$, whose stopped expectation is finite. For every open set $O$ of finite Lebesgue measure, exhaust $O$ by compact sets $K_j\uparrow O$. By [F4] choose $0\le\chi_j\le1$ smooth compactly supported in $O$, equal to one on $K_j$. The estimate in step 2.1 and $\|\chi_j\|_{d+1}\le|O|^{1/(d+1)}$ give $
u(K_j)\le C_d(1+E\int_0^\gamma| eta_s|ds)|O|^{1/(d+1)}$. Continuity from below gives the same bound for $
u(O)$. Every Lebesgue-null Borel set $N$ has open supersets of arbitrarily small finite measure by [F4], so monotonicity gives $
u(N)=0$. This argument needs no unproved inner-regularity assertion for $
u$.

The weight $Q_s(\det a_s)^{1/(d+1)}$ is strictly positive for $dt\otimes P$-almost every $s<\gamma$: the stopped trace integral is finite almost surely by its finite expectation, and $a_s\ge\kappa I$. For a null Borel set $N$, step 3.1 and Tonelli give a nonnegative random integral of that weight times $1_N(s,Z_s)$ equal to zero almost surely. Positivity of the weight then gives $\int_0^\gamma1_N(s,Z_s)ds=0$ almost surely, and taking expectations proves $\mu_\gamma(N)=0$. Finally take $\gamma_n=T\wedge\inf\{t:\int_0^t(|\beta_s|+\operatorname{tr}a_s)ds\ge n\}$, with infimum of the empty set interpreted as $T$. The integral is continuous adapted and finite on $[0,T]$, so these are stopping times, their stopped integrals are at most $n$, and for almost every path they equal $T$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Thus $\gamma_n\uparrow T$ and all the asserted stopped occupation measures are absolutely continuous.

boundaries.evidence: Proof step 3.1 gives nu(empty)=0 from the defining integral, and4.1 transfers nullness to mu; an empty time interval contributes zero dt mass.
The zero test f is harmless in1.1–step 2.1. A zero diffusion matrix is excluded by the Statement assumption a>=kappa I with kappa>0; no determinant-zero weight is divided out.
Dimension d=1 is covered directly by F1 and the scalar determinant; Proof step 2.1 uses the same square-energy estimate and3.1 the same open-set exponent1/(d+1).

Singular diffusion is outside the uniform ellipticity hypothesis. The pathwise trace may be unbounded, but Proof step 2.1 uses the positive discount Q and only finite expected stopped trace, not a deterministic upper bound.

Proof step 4.1 explicitly defines continuous cumulative-energy hitting times gamma_n, whose stopped integrals are at most n and which equal T eventually on each finite-energy path. Endpoints have zero dt mass.

AC is declared in Statement/A1 and supplied to the Bellman and Ito interfaces. Proof step 3.1 uses actual smooth cutoffs inside an open set; there is no choice of an occupation density or conditional version.

boundaries.reason: The Statement is a sufficient absolute-continuity conclusion, not an iff. Proof3.1 proves weighted nu(null)=0 by small open supersets, and4.1 proves positivity transfers this to mu(null)=0.
No converse ellipticity claim is made: absolute continuity alone is not asserted to imply uniform ellipticity. Proof4.1 uses kappa>0 only for the stated sufficient positive-weight argument.

risk_review.notes: Independently checked all four proof steps against the fully reviewed barrier and exact usual-filtration Ito/isometry, mollifier and outer-regularity interfaces. Convolve constant-control distribution inequalities first; continuity in A permits evaluation at the random positive matrix without evaluating weak derivatives on an unknown occupation measure. Discount Q cancels trace and zero-order terms. The uniform gradient bound and finite expected trace give a genuine mean-zero L2 stochastic term, while only L1 drift variation is used. Determinant weight is bounded by a constant times 1+trace, permitting the uniform f_epsilon limit. Compact cutoffs bound finite-measure open sets; outer regularity gives zero weighted occupation for every null Borel set without an inner-regularity import. Uniform ellipticity makes the weight strictly positive, giving unweighted absolute continuity. Continuous accumulated-energy stops reach T eventually. Bounded v at the initial point requires no Z0 moment, and no drift-square bound or auxiliary marginal law occurs. Singular a is excluded; time-zero atoms have zero occupation mass.
